speechtext: My hon. friend is a lawyer and I am not able to quibble with him on legal points. The fact is that Treadgold had that concession and he has not it now. The essential point of the statement of the Rev. Dr. Pringle was that Treadgold's ownership of that concession was an injury to the Yukon and I say Dr. Pringle was mistaken as the facts to-day prove. I say that the concession was of no value to Treadgold, that the Yukon is being developed to-day, not by the concession but by the investment of money made by the same Treadgold at another point and in another direction.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the concession were of no value to Treadgold so that the property could not be used, would not that of itself be an injury to the Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly not. If it was no good to Treadgold and no good to any body else what difference who owned it. If my hon. friend owned it to-day and if it could not be utilized by anybody, is the ownership of it hurting anybody. '

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Did it not tie up the property in the meantime ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, but so long as the property was of no value to anybody what difference did it make ? That is elementary and my hon. friend though a lawyer ought to know it.
Was the property tested?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know what property is in question ? It was not land, it was a water right. It was a question of investing money to bring that water into beneficial operation on the mining claims, and the engineering conditions were such that it could not be brought economically into beneficial operation on these claims.
That is what remained to be tested.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The evidence of that is that to-day Treadgold is bringing water

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: from another source altogether at a total expenditure of some $10,000,000. I am not finding any fault with Dr. Pringle for the view he took. I am merely suggesting he was mistaken in that view ; that he was absolutely and entirely mistaken.
As also was Treadgold.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As also was Treadgold ; as anybody is liable to be mistaken in a gold mining country.
They never know what is going to happen.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They never know what is going to happen until they get the gold in their pockets. Giving Dr. Pringle credit for good intentions, I say that Dr. Pringle is liable to be mistaken ; and here is one very clear instance in which he was absolutely mistaken. If my hon. friend was aware of the conditions of that country he has not the same excuse for offering' this quotation from Dr. Pringle's letter to the House to-day as a condemnation of the government, as Dr. Pringle had in writing it, because the events have proven that Dr. Pringle was wrong although my hon. friend did not inform the House on that point.
I had to give the whole document. My hon. friend would not have me read one part and omit another part.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not finding fault with what my hon. friend said. He was making a partisan presentation of the case and he took advantage of this statement which Dr. Pringle made years ago before the knowledge had come, and he was using that statement to create the impression that that condition existed to-day. If he was aware of the facts

I do not say he was-he must have known that it did not exist and that Dr. Pringle was mistaken when he made that statement.

I suppose my hon. friend does not want to be unfair to Dr. Pringle, and would not like it to go out that Dr. Pringle was mistaken in that statement. Dr. Pringle, as the minister agrees, was right in his statement of the facts at that time, but was not right in his appreciation of what might happen from them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He was right in a part of his facts, but not in the whole of them.
I imagine that he was right in the whole of his facts, but not in his anticipations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He stated his anticipations as facts, in the most emphatic language. The Yukon is a very important territory, and it is not necessarily surrounded with that air of mystery which my hon. friend suggested, and which seemed to be such a

source of enjoyment to him. The Yukon is a business proposition, and it is desirable in the interests of every j>art of Canada that it should be fully and properly developed. Tile value of the Yukon is in its gold production. When gold was discovered there the means whereby that gold production could be made most effective, most economically, was under the consideration of the government of the day. In a vast country like tlie Yukon no government could expect, and this government did not expect, that there was abundance of gold everywhere. While there was abundance of gold in one or two or three locations, a great balance of the area contained either no gold or a limited quantity of gold. Therefore in their mining regulations they made provision not only for the mining of the limited area where gold was abundant, but also for other areas where gold was less abundant ; that is to say. they provided for miners' claims and for hydraulic concessions. Rev. Dr. Pringle, in this letter written in 1902, declares most strongly against hydraulic concessions, declaring them to be iniquitous, and holds the government responsible for tile iniquity of the policy, as he was perfectly right in doing if it was iniquitous. The principle underlying that policy was an absolutely sound principle, a principle which it is necessary to recognize in the securing of the gold production of that country. Any policy that does not recognize the necessity of providing for the development of the vast areas of low-grade values in that country is not an effective or sound policy. It is possible that, owing to lack of knowledge of the conditions at the time, the administration with regard to the hydraulic concessions was not all that could be desired ; but the idea that is attempted to be conveyed by Dr. Pringle, that the principle of hydraulic concessions was a principle of corrupt dealings, intended to bar out the individual and to advance the interests of corrupt friends of the government, had absolutely no foundation in fact ; and my hon. friend, in using Dr. rringle's letter to place that same idea before the House, is in exactly the same position as Dr. Pringle.
There is just one other allusion I want to make to these long letters of Dr. Pringle's. In the letter of January 3, 1905, he deals with conditions as he considers he finds them at that time, particularly with the circumstances surrounding the election of Dr. Thompson, the sitting member for the Yukon, and he gives his opinion, in good free terms, of the gentleman who was or claimed to be, the government candidate, and of the methods by which he attempted to secure election. I want to read one line of this letter, because I think it is desirable that the House should have its attention drawn to it in view of further or future letters written by Dr. Pringle. He is dealing with the expenditure of money, asserting that the money of the country was being administered under the Yukon government with a view to advancing the interests of those who were likely to support Mr. Congdon. This he particularly charges was the case in regard to road works, and he says :
It is am open secret that Mr. Bertrand would ha.vc started ia road around the cliff to Moosehide, to cost about $15,COO had not Mr. Lithgow (refused to be responsible for the expenditure.
Mr. Lithgow was the controller of the territory, what might be called the Finance Minister of the government as it then was, and Dr. Pringle declares that Mr. Lithgow, in the discharge of what he believed to be his duty in his official position on that occasion. saved the government of the country $15,000 which he charges it was desired to expend corruptly in the interests of the election of the government candidate. That is the same Mr. Lithgow whom in his letters of last year, he charged with divers and sundry crimes and misdemeanours, which I think was very little to the credit of the gentleman making the charges.

Will the minister allow me one remark there ? That seems to me to show a spirit of eminent fairness in Dr. Pringle. He gave to Mr. Lithgow the full credit of stopping the illegal expenditure. When it comes to other sides of Mr. Lith-gow's character, he prefers his charges.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Dr. Pringle at that time did not make any charges against Mr. Lithgow. His charges in 1905 were against Mr. Congdon and his supporters. Mr. Lithgow apparently was not one of Mr. Congdon's supporters, and therefore he has no charges against him, and the simple statement was made that Mr. Lithgow had prevented an improper expenditure of $15,000. Either the statement that Mr. Bertrand wanted to expend $15,000 improperly is untrue, or the statement that Mr. Lithgow prevented that is untrue. He can have it either way.
Which way is it ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I say he can have it either way. I do not think it is either way. I am not entitled to accept his statement.
You are not in a position to deny it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not in a position to deny it, but I do not accept it. There is nothing in these letters to warrant an acceptance of their general allegations. 1 have pointed out one or two cases in which they are very wide of the mark, and where a gentleman uses such strong language as Dr Pringle does, the chances are that he has gone wide of the mark in more cases than one.
Dr. Pringle wrote in 1905 and received a

reply, but he finds fault because he is not given a copy of the reply which Mr. Goiig-dou sent to the department. I want to point out in this connection that when the government received Mr. Pringle's letter in the beginning of 1905, the government at once asked Mr. Congdon what reply he had to make to it. It was not therefore a case in which the government was letting the matter rest. The demand for a reply from Mr. Congdon was immediate and so was his reply, and in my humble judgment his reply was conclusive. It seems to me that the case was then closed. The government had inquired into it and the allegations had not only been denied but disproved. And there was nothing further to be done. And I am not aware that Dr. Pringle had any particular or inherent right to be given a copy of the letter sent by Mr. Congdon. He had seen fit to make a statement, the government had made inquiry, and it was for the government to decide whether it was satisfied or not.
What inquiry did the government make ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It inquired from Mr. Congdon, who was the man charged by Dr. Pringle with impropriety in the conduct of the election. Mr. Congdon's reply was, in my judgment, conclusive.
Why then was Mr. Henderson appointed to investigate ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend is mixing up his dates. That was subsequent. Mr. Henderson was not appointed until the summer of 1907 and Mr. Pringle's charge and Mr. Congdon's reply were in 1905. The matter rested there until the necessity came to appoint a commissioner to the Yukon in succession to Mr. Mclnnis. In the interval between the beginning of 1905 and 1907, Mr. Mclnnis had been appointed commissioner, and after having served a certain time he resigned and we had to appoint a successor. Mr. Lithgow's name was mentioned favourably for the vacancv by some of his friends in the Yukon. His name was forwarded in nomination for the position, and Dr. Pringle, having heard I presume of this recommendation, came out with another letter in which he gave his opinion of Mr. Lithgow and matters and things generally in the Yukon. His letter was written to myself and replied to. Dr. Prinsrle's letter was dated 19th January, and is as follows :
I am ashamed to think that the impression will go abroad that the people of the Yukon are willing to have such a man as Lithgow as commissioner, much lo^s to request the government to appoint him. His life here has been a public scandal, and while if he were a private citizen, I should have nothing to say excent to himself, as a public official and one evidently seekinv the highest position in this territory in the people's gift, he is or>en to the judgment of any citizen Mr. OLIVER.
He says that Mr. Lithgow's life was a public scandal, and after a long statement to that effect, concludes :
Last night a meeting for the purpose of promoting Mr. Lithgow's interests was called by his friends who are for the most part those who surrounded Congdon. The meeting was overwhelmingly anti-Lithgow. Many did not vote, but it showed 97 to 73 against Lithgow.

In that letter there is no suggestion of an attack on Mr. Lithgow because of any act in his position as controller. The attack is based wholly on the possibility of his appointment as commissioner. That letter was promptly replied to and did not call for further action ; but on the 31st July 1907, the Rev. Mr. Pringle comes forward with his charges against Mr. Lithgow and Mi. Girouard in their positions as government officials.

Is the minister correct in that ?
Mr- OLIVER. That is as I understand
If my hon. friend will look, he will find that the charge against Girouard, substantiated by affidavits, was made in 1905 by Mr. Pringle.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Possibly, I am speaking of the correspondence addressed to myself and of which I have personal knowledge.
Mr. Pringle's letters of 1905 were also addressed to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I was not minister at the time ; but if this letter was addressed to the then Minister of the Interior in the early part of 1905, I myself visited the Yukon during that period. I visited that country for the purpose of looking into the conditions for myself, and I am bound to say that neither Mr. Pringle nor any one else in or about the Yukon gave me any hint or indication of any such charges such as have been made in the letter. It appears to me that if the conditions were so bad and urgent as represented, it would have been only reasonable and fair that I should have been informed of them at the time and in the place where I was for the express purpose of seeing and hearing all I could with regard to the administration in the Yukon.
They might have been a little frightened.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Will the minister read the charges as shown on page 14 ? I think that he and the House will find they are tolerably specific.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are tolerably specific.
I think they are verv specific.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the point I want tile House to come to. Well, I do not wish to discredit ' Hansard ' by reading the wording of this statement unless my hon. friend insists.
I do not insist if you only admit they are specific.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not admit they are specific, and if the hon. gentleman insists they are I will have to read them to show they are not specific, and that they are not in a form which will enable any man to come forward and disprove them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He would not come forward to disprove the charges ; he would come forward t,o disprove the evidence that was brought in support of them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend forgets he is in parliament and not in a court.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman knows where he is.
Suppose the party who makes the charges produces credible evidence to prove them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not learned in the law, but I think we all know enough about
the law to know that when I bring a complaint against you I have to state the time and place and occasion, and the reason for that is so that you may have an opportunity of disproving that charge in particular and in general. Unless time and place and occasion are given you have not a fair opportunity to disprove my charge. In this case Dr. Pringle does not give time and place and location. He says that certain things occurred but he does not put that assertion in such shape that Mr. Lithgow or Mr. Girouard could come forward and say : That is false, I was not there at that time or place. Under this statement of Dr. Pringle, Mr. Lithgow and Mr. Girouard would have to prove a negative covering an indeterminate period of it might be one week, or one month, or six months, or five years as the case might be, and I submit that is not a fair or reasonable proposition.
Did the minister read the particulars of the affidavits with reference to Girouard ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not going to read them.
It seems to me he would find them very particular as to date, as to place, as to circumstance.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But these are not Hie statements of Dr. Pringle and it is Dr. Pringle I am dealing with now.
I thought it was Dr. Pringle's evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am dealing with Dr. Pringle and the statement he made, and I am arguing in defence of the position I took in dealing with this question, and I want to show the House and the country that the position I took was fair. I want to point out that the statements made by Dr. Pringle were not in specific form such as would be fair and reasonable to enable the men who are charged with these offences to absolutely disprove them. I say that the man who makes a general charge such as that is not acting fairly towards the person against whom he makes it. And I say that charged with my responsibility 1 would not be warranted in doing otherwise than offering Dr. Pringle an opportunity to come forward and make specific statements as to these charges before I would have further proceedings in the matter. Fair play is bonnie play, and while Messrs. Lithgow and Girouard may he people living aw'ay in the Yukon, they may be discreditable or creditable. In the position which I occupy it is not for me to consider where they are or who they are or what they are, but to give them just the same square deal that any white man is entitled to in this country. I don't think I was entitled to do otherwise than to require, before taking further proceedings, that Dr. Pringle should
9G27

say when, where and how these transactions took place so as to give these men a fair and reasonable opportunity to disprove the charges if they could.

Does the minister pretend to say that under a royal commission issued by parliament to inquire into the conduct of officials charged with wrong-doing, it is necessary to state specific dates and specific instances ? Does he think that yon should lay a complaint in such a case as you would lay a complaint before a magistrate ? Does he think that was done in the case of McGreevy and Connolly, who were charged with certain offences in connection with public works ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I take issue with that position here and now and I do it ,on my responsibility as a member and as a minister. As I understand it the very foundation principle of British justice is that there shall be no trial unless there is an accusation. Whatever may be the view of parliament on any special occasion, or of the Governor in Council on any special occasion, for myself in the administration of my office I have not taken any other view, and I may inform the House and the country that I do not propose to take any other view than that there shall be a charge before there shall be an investigation.
Why then did the minister appoint Mr. Henderson to make an investigation ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To give Dr. Pringle an opportunity to make his statements specific so that there could be an investigation. I further gave Mr. Henderson authority to make inquiries as to the general or specific conduct of any official in the Yukon.
Which he did not do.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Which he has reported to me in his letter, that he did, and that he has nothing to report as to misconduct on their part.

Does the minister regard it as necessary that a charge must be made specifically against an official with regard to date, time, and incident ? Does he think he is doing the proper thing to go pn with an inquiry and not allow the witnesses to be either subpoenaed or sworn, but take their ipse dixit ; and is he willing to accept that as evidence but not allow the commission he has appointed to put these witnesses on oath ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When the charge is made specific, when a statement is made which is capable of being proven or disproven as a question of fact-then is the time we will take to put witnesses on oath, and until that specific statement is made, I say I am not warranted, as a matter of fair play, in putting it in the power of a man who Mr. OLIVER.
is unwilling to make such a specific charge to compel this or that citizen to come forward and make a statement under oath concerning matters on which, perhaps, he has no information or, perhaps, concerning which he does not wish to speak.

But he says:	Give
such a commission and I will make a charge, but until you do that I will not make a charge. He probably has a reason for that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I say that, until he makes a specific charge, I will not give him an inquiry under oath, but if he does make his charge specific the question of an inquiry under oath will be one for consideration. That is a point I want to make absolutely and positively clear.
Mr, FOSTER. That is the policy of the government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is my policy in administering this department in this connection. I want that distinctly understood. While I want to see honest officials and clean administration, I will not be a party to a system of simple slander which will discredit honourable men-or dishonourable or any other kind of men-without anybody being responsible for the circulation of the slander.

Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) think that he ought to be higher or greater authority than parliament ? Take the example of what this House has done in the Hodgins case. A committee has been appointed to inquire into certain allegations that have appeared in the press, and we give the committee charged with that duty power to swear every witness who comes before it and bring out all the information under oath, though the charges are only of a general character and though neither dates nor specific instances are alleged. Parliament is supposed to he a model in what It does with regard to inquiries or anything else. Does the minister think he is a higher authority than parliament or what parliament does it is not proper for him to do ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think that parliament has a higher authority than I have, and that what may be perfectly justifiable for parliament may not be justifiable for me, that what may be justifiable action on the part of parliament in the prosecution of the public business would not necessarily be justifiable in me in the investigation of the private character of an individual. Parliament is supreme ; parliament can do what it pleases ; parliament can be unjust if it likes ; parliament can make any inquiry it wishes to make, but I say that even parliament has no right to set up an inquisition into the private character of individuals. Still, even if parliament had such a right, it would not follow that I have that right. I do not pretend to such
-TUNE 2, 1908
a right, and I do not propose to exercise it. I say distinctly that I do not propose to make myself a party to any general scheme of slander, let it be put forward by any person, minister of the gospel or any other. If a slander is uttered, the best I can do is to afford the man who utters it an opportunity to prove what he has stated, to substantiate it by any evidence he may bring forward, to choose his own time, his own place, his own occasion, and if he will not do that, if he will not choose time, place and occasion so that the party accused can disprove the accusation, if it be a thing that can be disproved, I think I have discharged my duty, as I have said in my letter to the Rev. Dr. Pringle, and I believe that the country will sustain me in that position.
I think the country will reach a different conclusion.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think that, because men live in the Yukon they are less entitled to the rights of Canadian citizenship than are those who live in Toronto, or Ottawa or elsewhere. I deal with all Canadian citizens in the same way. I want to say that it seems to me it has been the habit in discussing this question of the Yukon to discuss it with the idea that the man who has taken his life in his hand, who has risked his all and his life every day in the reclaiming of the wilderness and the building up of the country-this man, merely because he is a pioneer, is to be regarded as less than the ordinary kind of man and that he is not entitled to the same consideration as other people. I want to say to this House, and I will say it to the country, that so far as I am concerned the pioneer is the man whose interests require first attention at the hands of this government, of this country, of this people ; and that, because a man is a pioneer in the Yukon, because a man is a gold miner, he is none the less a citizen of Canada and none the less entitled to every consideration that every other citizen of Canada is entitled to. Because Dawson is in the Yukon the citizens of that city are not less entitled to fair-play, honest treatment, fair consideration, they are not less entitled to being spoken of fairly and decently, than are the citizens of Toronto or Ottawa. Now, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how would such a proposition as tliis^ which has been suggested by Rev. Dr. Pringle be received if applied to the city of Toronto or the city of Ottawa? That a slander should be uttered against a citizen of Toronto or Ottawa, that it should be declared that his private conduct was not such as it ought to be, and because he held an office from the city or from the province or from the Dominion, therefore there must be an inquiry by royal commission into whether it is true or false. It would be absurd. No man
would justify such a proposition applied to Toronto or Ottawa. Why then apply it to the Yukon?
That is the case as it has struck me- we must give to people who are living in the Yukon the same consideration as we are giving to people anywhere else, and that to trespass upon the rights of a citizen of the Yukon, whether a government official or a private citizen, is just the same as to trepass on the rights of a citizen of Toronto or Ottawa. And Rev. Dr. Pringle has no more right to circulate throughout this country allegations that this man or that man is not correct in his private life than any reverend gentleman in Ottawa would have to circulate such statements regarding the members of this House or regarding any other citizen.
It is said that there is vice in the Yukon. It is said that there is crime in the Yukon. The evidence is that there is less crime in the Yukon, man for man, than there is possibly right here in Ottawa. As to vice,
I am not able to answer. But it is certainly a notorious fact that the city of Ottawa is not free from vice-that the city of Toronto is not free from vice-that the city of Montreal is not free from vice. Why should not parliament concern itself with the morals of the city of Montreal as well as with the morals of the city of Dawson? It seems to me that there is a wrong point of view in regard to this question of the conditions in tlie Yukon and in regard to the observance of law and morality there. It is unquestionable that, from the establishment of the authority of the Canadian government in the Yukon, there has been a most phenomenal maintenance of law and order, of enforcement of the rights of life and property. No one can gainsay that. When you consider the facts in the Yukon along with those in Alaska immediately across the line, the comparison is simply [DOT]startling.

May I ask the minister a question? If that be so, how does he account for the fact that we have paid for a number of years $500,000 for a police force to look after the people up there-$500,000 for a police force for 8,000 people?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I say that the maintenance of law and order in the Yukon
That is what the police are for.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, they are there, and they maintain law and order.
Is there any portion of Canada where the condition of things is anything like that ?
Order.
What does the hon. gentleman say? I do not think the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) ought to be so needlessly offensive.
Somebody ought to ; it is time. You had better sit down now.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Mounted Police are maintained in the Yukon by the country for the purpose of keeping law and order. They have kept law and order. So, that,
I say, the contrast between the conditions in the Yukon and in the immediately adjoining territory of Alaska, in so far as law and order are concerned, and in so far as protection to life and property are concerned, is simply startling. There is no consideration given to that fact. Conditions are painted in the Yukon with regard to vice and immorality, which conditions exist, I say, in every city of the Dominion and in every city of the world, xt is a matter of regret that these conditions do exist. It is to be regretted that they exist in Dawson, but they do not exist any more in Dawson than can be helped. The authorities are as energetic in suppressing this condition in Dawson as they are anywhere else, but because they are not successful in Dawson, as they are not successful anywhere else in the world, is no reason why the people of the Yukon should be slandered in general or in particular.
Mr. iSPROULE. Is it a fact that you will have an equally good condition of affairs in a country where you have one hotel selling liquor for every ninety-four of the people as you will in a country where there is only one hotel for every thousand people. The former was the condition that they had in Dawson a few years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
On the other hand it must be remembered that there Is a good deal of difference between the conditions in Dawson and the conditions in other places. The conditions in Dawson were at that time that there was an immense aggregation of men engaged in active, energetic, outdoor employment with plenty of money to spend and limited opportunities for spending it. I do not know that there were more opportunities for getting liquor in Dawson in proportion to the class of men who took liquor than there were in any part of Ontario ; because, it must be remembered that in Ontario the proportion of men who are of the class which I have described is very limited as compared with the whole population whereas in Dawson they are the whole population. There is no use of comparing conditions unless you compare like conditions, unless you compare the conditions that existed in Dawson with similar conditions elsewhere. However, I am not apologizing or saying anything with regard to the conditions as to the sale of liquor. That is a matter within the regulation of the Yukon Council itself. It is in accordance with the public opinion Mr. SPROULE.
of the people of the Yukon. Perhaps they are wrong. If I had to answer the question I would say that they were absolutely wrong and that is their business and they must transact that business as best they may and according to their own judgment.
1 will not repeat the slanders which have been uttered by the Rev. Dr. Pringle with regard to Mr. Lithgow's private character and I will only revert to the certificate that he gave in these very letters to Mr. Lith-gow with reference to his character as a public official. A man who, as he says, saved the country $15,000, even though there was pressure upon him to allow the expenditure to be made in the heat of an election when a supporter of the government was concerned, is the man that he asks us to condemn, that he asks us to put out of his position where he has served a useful purpose during all these years and he asks us to do so because he chooses to repeat a slander that he heard against him. When he was given an opportunity to give us the proof he was not able to get the people who had given him the story to come forward and say it was true. Under these circumstances we could not do other than we have done. If we are to listen to every attack that might be made upon every officer of the government in his private capacity we are not giving that credit to good service that good service is entitled to. Let me allude to the suggestion that the hon. member for North Toronto made as to the difference between the treatment given the demand for an investigation by Dr. Pringle and the demand for an investigation by a Mr. Perron who complained of some mishandling of his affairs in the Gold Commissioner's office. The difference between the conditions was this : The complaint of Mr. Perron was in regard to public business and Mr. Perron was entitled to a commission under the terms of the Act.
Would the minister mind stating what was the business ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It was something in connection with priority in the filing of a certain document. I have just forgotten the actual facts. It was a matter of the transaction of public business. The Act expressly says :
The minister presiding over any department of the civil service of Canada, may appoint at any time, under the authority of the Governor in Council, a commissioner or commissioners to investigate and report upon the state and management of the business, or any part of the business, of such department, either in the inside or outside service thereof, and the conduct of any person in such service, so far as the same relates to his official duties.
The charge made by Mr. Perron related to the official duty of a certain member of the service and under that section an in-

vestigation was lield. I submit that the charges made by Mr. Pringle against Mr. Lithgow and Mr. Girouard are not charges in regard to their official duties and that therefore this section does not give authority to hold a commission upon these charges.

The minister is wrong with reference to the charge made against Mr. Girouard. I think that absolutely and definitely refers to his official duties. He should have been somewhere and he was somewhere else.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I beg my hon. friend's pardon. I am afraid we will have to read these charges in order to satisfy him.
If you read the affidavits you will find it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But there were no affidavits.
Yes, there were six of them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Given by Dr. Pringle ?
(Mr. FOSTER. Yes, sent by Dr. Pringle to the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am speaking of the charges amde by Mr. Pringle, in 1907.
What's the odds as between 1907 and 1905 ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The odds is this that I ordered an investigation into the charges made in 1907, and if Dr. Pringle had these affidavits in his possession all he had to do was to put them before the commission. I do not know why he did not do so. He did not do so although we gave him the opportunity to do so.
He told you why.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But he did not do so at any rate. He refused to do it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why would the affidavits be any better in the possession of the commissioner than in the possession of the government ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The government appointed a commissioner to hold an investigation and when a commissioner is appointed to hold an investigation it is through his hands formally that everything has to be done.
The commissioner asked the minister for a commission ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know he did and that is a point in regard to which the commissioner and I differed. As he was the commissioner, my view, for the time being, prevailed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Only for a short time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot read the section in any other way. It is provided that there 306
shall be a commission of inquiry into the conduct of any person only so far as the same relates to his official duties. We have granted commissions to inquire into matters affecting the official duties of officials in the Yukon. We have not granted a royal commission to inquire into the private conduct of any official in the Yukon, but when allegations against the private conduct of any official were made, although they were not specific and although they were not substantiated by evidence, an opportunity was given both to make them specific and to substantiate them by evidence. While I do not wish to load up ' Hansard ' it might be just as well to read the conclusion of the correspondence between the commissioner and myself so that It may be available to the public. On the 2nd of January, 1908, I wrote the commissioner :
Ottawa, January 2, 1908.
Dear Sir,-T have before me the papers in connection with the inquiry ordered in respect of Dr. Pringle's charges with your covering letter of December 7.
I note that in your letter of November 8 you suggest your appointment as a commissioner to investigate the charges under the provisions of the Inquiries Act, chapter 101, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906.
In reply to this suggestion I beg to say that it appears to me that it would be a very strained construction to put upon section 2 of that Act to say that an inquiry into charges of the nature of those made by Dr. Pringle was an inquiry * into and concerning any matter connected with the good government of Canada or the conduot of any part of the public business thereof.' Masmuch as Dr. Pringle has been requested to make a specific statement of his knowledge of the facts regarding which he complains, and has failed to do so, I do not think I would be warranted in applying the terms of the Inquiries Act.
If Dr. Pringle had availed himself of the opportunity which you gave him under my instructions, it would then _ be a matter for consideration whether we might or might not invoke the terms of the Act, but without something more definite than has yet been brought to your attention, I do not think we have suflicient warrant for doing so.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) FRANK OLIVER. Hon. Alexander Henderson,
Commiisisoner Yukon Territory, Dawson.
I followed that with another letter on the 9th of January, as follows :
Ottawa, January 9, 1908.
Dear Sir,

Your report of December 7 on charges made by Dr. Pringle against Messrs. Lithgow and Girouard has been duly received.
I note your statement that both Messrs. Lithgow and Girouard have emphatically denied to you the truth of the charges. I also note the refusal of Dr. Pringle, when offered the opportunity, to make such further statements in connection with his charges as would be necessary to enable you to reach a



conclusion; also your statement that no other person in the territory had made any charges to you with respect to either of the officials named; that yon had seen nothing in the conduct of either of them which would warrant the conclusion that the charges made by Dr. Pringle against them, or either of them, could be substantiate!; and also that Mr. Girouard has commenced an action against Dr. Pringle for damages for libel, and that the action is now pending.
In yiew of these facts, and as you have no authority to hold an inquiry under oath, 9Uch as Dr. Pringle desires, it does not seem to me that the ease at present calls for further action on your part.
At the same time I desire it to he distinctly understood that in case of there coming to your knowledge such personal actions of any official of this government in the Yukon Territory as would or might constitute a publio scandal, or as to refleot unfavourably upon this government you are expected to report the oa.se to me fully and without delay so that the government may he in a position to deal with such official as the circumstances seem to warrant.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) PRANK OLIVER. Hon. Alexander Henderson,
Commissioner Yukon District, Dawson, Yukon Territory.
Does the minister know what was the result of the action for slander ; was it prosecuted ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say. I presume the courts will deal with it.
Is Mr. Girouard now an officer of the government ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Girouard is not an officer of the government at the present time. Mr. Girouard applied to leave the government service and the office he held has been consolidated with another office in the interests of economy.
Who holds the consolidated office ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Lalibertfi was librarian of the Justice Department and he now holds the dual position of librarian and registrar at the former salary of the registrar. In conclusion I want to say that I think there should be a very wide distinction drawn-at any rate I want to draw a very wide distinction-between allegations made against the public and against the private conduct of any official. I am quite aware that a man is the same man in public as in private, and I am quite aware that it is to the credit of the government and to the credit of the country that its officials should conduct themselves so that there should not be any scandal attaching to their names while they are in the public service. I do not think there is any person in this House who is more thoroughly imbued with that idea than I am. But, as was stated in Mr. OLIVER
the quotation from the ' Globe this is not a question of the conduct of Messrs. Girouard and Lithgow ; this is a question of whether a royal commission should be appointed by a responsible minister to find out whether an official of his department had conducted himself properly in his private capacity. In regard to that I want to say that I hold myself responsible to the House and to the country for the private conduct of the officials of tile department which I have the honour to administer so far as that private conduct can be considered to come in collision with public interest or public duty, and for my part I do not need any royal commission to tell me what to do in the case of an official in the employ of the Interior Department, whose private conduct is such as to reflect discredit upon the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Minister of the Interior has treated us to one of his old time extraordinary speeches which fortunately are becoming less and less frequent the longer he continues in office. When he seeks to cast discredit on Dr. Pringle, naturally he does not allude to the circumstances that four years ago he and his party were perfectly ready to exploit that reverend gentleman's name for the purpose of clearing themselves from odium in connection with the Yukon. But now that this gentleman has made certain statements, first in 1002, again in 1905 and afterwards in 1907, the minister while preserving a certain appearance of fairness has endeavoured before the House and the country to cast that discredit upon Dr. Pringle which is hardly consistent with the fair play for which he himself cried out so vehemently in his address. The minister asks for fair play. Does he think it is fair play to the people of Canada or to the people of the Yukon or to his own officials, that he should make a mockery of the investigation he pretended to carry on in regard to the charges made by Dr. Pringle ? I endeavoured during the course of his remarks to find a single line of intelligible thought in the mind of the minister with regard to the course that ought to be pursued, and I say in all candour that I was absolutely unable to find it. I do not think any hon. gentleman in this House will be able to extract from the remarkable address of the minister any comprehensible line of thought as to the duty of a public man in regard to officials under such circumstances. My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) came under the censure of the Minister of the Interior. My hon. friend exercised a remarkable control in dealing with this matter. He over and over again as I know-because having a copy of the return before me I followed

him-left out passages that he might very well have read had he desired only to east discredit upon the administration of this government. There was no attempt by the hon. member, except to put forward a few of the least, but not any of the worst of the abominations and deviltries that have been carried on in the Yukon under the administration of this government and by certain officials of this government during the past six or seven years.
I do not desire at the present moment to speak of the allegations of Dr. Pringle so far as they concern the remarkable concessions granted in the Yukon or the policy of the government in regard to the development of that country. I will not even refer to liis charges in respect of the manner in ,which the election in 1904 was carried on, although it is perfectly well known to any one who has come in contact with men from the Yukon, that not only in that election, but in the first election in the Yukon, exactly that kind of work was carried on. In the first election there were two polling places established near the American boundary, and eight or ten men were brought over from the other side of the line. They went up and voted. Five minutes afterwards they went up and voted again under other names ; and so they continued, with the result that in places where there were not more than five or six people living, the then member for the Yukon had a majority of between 300 and 400, if I am correctly informed, a majority greater than the total majority by which he was returned.
But these are not the important parts of the statement of Dr. Pringle. His statements concern, in the first place, the administration of the Yukon by this government. I will take for the purpose of my argument simply one challenge by Dr. Pringle with respect to the administration of that country by this government. Let us look at what he says in his letter of the 3rd of January, 1905, with respect to the carrying on under the sanction of this government of what are known as dance halls in the Yukon-licensed dance halls :
I found that the administration had been a disgrace to the Canadian name, such as no self-respecting Canadian could excuse.
I may say that throughout Dr. Pringle's letters he seems to have noting but good words for the endeavours of Mr. Ross, now Senator Ross, to bring about decency and public order in that country. He says further :
In July, 1902, Mr. Ross practically compelled the passage of an ordinance suppressing the dance halls, the women in which were the most dangerous class of prostitutes, and absolutely excluding lewd women from licensed liquor houses.
That was the work of Mr. Ross, the condition of whose health, I understand, corn-3064
pelled him afterwards to leave that country, so that he was not responsible for the condition that supervened after his departure.
In September of the same year, Mr. Ross lying unconscious at Whitehorse, the ordinance was amended at the instance of the legal adviser, now Judge Newlands, so as to render the ordinance abortive, hut under Mr. Cong-don's lead we have legalized the dance halls. Some government officials are their habitues.
And further on :
The sergeant of the town station tells me that fifty per cent of the licensed houses are houses of prostitution.
There is a distinct charge by Dr. Pringle -in the first place, that these dance houses were carried on as houses of prostitution; in tlie second place, that Mr. Ross, then Commissioner of file Yukon, had put them down ; in the third place, that Mr. Newlands. afterwards elevated to the bench by the government of this country, had introduced an amendment into the ordinances of the Yukon which practically rendered nugatory Mr. Ross's efforts ; and, in the fourth place, that afterwards Mr. Congdon gave full swing to these dance houses by permitting them to he carried on under the sanction of tlie government. Has the Minister of tlie Interior any denial of the truth of what Dr. Pringle stated as to the character of these houses ? Though he has not a word of denial, I will answer him out of the mouth of his owu officials in the Yukon to-day. Instead of endeavouring to cast aspersions upon Dr. rringle, as he has done, lie and every other member of that government ought to he grateful to this man for raising the agitation which has resulted in the abolition of dance halls in the Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman inform the House by whose legislation the dance halls have been abolished ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I will show that as a result of tlie agitation brought about by Dr. Pringle they have been abolished by Ml-. Henderson, since lie has been there as commissioner. That is my answer to the minister ; does he regard it as satisfactory ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is satisfactory as far as it goes, hilt it is hardly correct.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: For his information I will read the evidence of one of the hon. gentleman's officials, in order that he may be convinced that he does not know everything about liis own department or even about the Yukon which he pretends to govern.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To save the hon. gentleman trouble, I will say that the dance halls were abolished, not by Mr. Henderson, but by ordinance of tlie Yukon council.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Which Mr. Henderson brought about The minister may talk

about lawyers' quibbles, but I know no man more given to them than the hon. gentleman himself.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the Speaker control the legislation of this parliament ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, but the government having the majority of the members of the Yukon council, control them, and the commissioner, I suppose, can exercise a certain influence on the men appointed by this government to bring about legislation, and therefore, did it in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The commissioner is the speaker of the council.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister persists in his quibbling. I will not pursue the matter further.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that members of the council appointed by the government, such as Judge Dugas, are open to political influences ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Beyond question they are under the control of this government, and they have carried out the policy of this government ever since they have been in the Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman explain for the information of the House just how Judge Dugas is under the control of this government in his action ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It does not make the slightest difference to me whether his action was under the control of the government or not. The point I make is that the abolition of the dance halls was brought about as a result of the agitation carried on by Dr. Pringle. I have read the evidence of an official of this government, and I will proceed to read the evidence of an official of the Northwest Mounted Police, bearing date the 7tli December, 1907.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Before we get away from the point as to the right of this government to control the legislation of the Yukon council. I think it would be interesting to the House and the country to have that point settled. The hon. gentleman has suggested that the appointed members of the council are subject to the authority of this government in their legislation. I may ask him, since Judge Dugas' name has been mentioned, to what extent is Judge Dugas' action in the council of the Yukon subject to the control of this government ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is subject in this way, that this government, so long as it keeps that council under its control, is supposed to have its policy carried out by that council. If any member of that council does not see fit to carry out the policy of this government in that connection, he is in the same position as would be a member of Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
the cabinet who did not find himself in accord with the policy of the government as a w7hole. He would find it necessary to leave that council just as a dissenting minister would have to leave the cabinet. If my hon. friend does not agree with me, I am sorry that we differ, but the point is a very subsidiary one. Instead of cavilling at Mr. Pringle, this government ought to be grateful to him for having started and carried out an agitation which has brought about the dissolution of these dance halls in the Yukon. The government should have expressed their gratitude to Dr. Pringle, rather than endeavour to cast aspersions on the gentleman who has brought about that very good reform.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I want to have the credit placed where it belongs. The dance halls were abolished by the legislation of the Yukon council and not by the authority of this government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am glad to have the minister make practically the admission that if the policy of this government had been carried out, the dance halls would not have been abolished.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not make that admission.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not know what else the hon. gentleman's words mean. I would have supposed that'the government were in accord with the policy of_ the Yukon council in that regard, but the minister makes it clear that, for some reason or other not apparent, he desired to have these dance halls continued.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot allow my hon. friend to suggest that anything I have said is open to any such construction. I say that the Yukon council, ,on its own responsibility and by its otvn authority, abolished the dance halls and that it was not this parliament or government that abolished them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am reading from a letter of the 7th December, 1907, from Mr. T. A. Wroughton, commanding 1B ' division of the Royal Northw'est Mounted Police, to the assistant commissioner of that corps, and dated from Dawson, Yukon Territory :
Royal Northwest Mounted Police.
' B ' Division.
Dawson, Y.T., December 7, 1907. The Assistant Commissioner,
R. N. W. M. Police, Yukon Territory, Dawson, Yukon Territory.
Sir-I have the honour to report, pursuant to your instructions, as follows, with regard to the alleged social evils in Dawson.
Formerly, while dance halls were permitted to exist under a licensed system, they were undoubtedly hot beds of evil; women were encouraged to frequent these places by the glare and glitter and a life of comparative

luxury as compared wit h the lives of their hardworking and honest sisters. These women were ostensibly under salary, whereas as a matter of fact the salary they received was a mere subterfuge, their real pay being derived from the monetary percentage they derived from the price of drinks, &c., which they were enabled to persuade the customers to buy. Time and again cases have been prosecuted in the courts, but we were unable to get convictions; we were confronted with the cleverest legal talent that money could procure (these people always appeared to have unlimited capital at their backs.) Time and again we spent money and energy in working up cases, employing special men (stool pigeons) but always with the same result.
The last attempt we made in the percentage cases was as strong a case as we could possibly hope to get (this was the opinion oi the Crown prosecutor) but what with perjured evidence and advantage taken of every technicality we failed. Naturally the class of men we have to employ (our regular men being too well known to conduct this species of work) was not of the highest order, and this the defence never failed to bring forward.
The last assembly of the Yukon council, however, repealed the objectionable ordinance with the result that conditions are much improved. The principal dance hall has gone out of business, and the only one remaining is trying to keep up its end on the sale of temperance beverages, and is, I am informed, tottering -to its fall. It was said that intoxicants were sold on this side; I have employed detectives on the matter who report that such is not the case.
That is the report of this officer of the police regarding the character ,of these dance halls. Let us look at what Mr. Henderson says about his action in the matter. The minister, as I understand, denies that this reform was brought about through the action of Dr. Pringle. I am reading from a letter of Mr. Henderson, being his report, under date of the Ttli December, 1907, to the Minister of the Interior :
Before my arrival in the territory I ha6 heard that the question of dance halls had been brought prominently before the public through a letter addressed to a Winnipeg newspaper by the Reverend Dr. Pringle, and I felt that one of the first questions which would demand my attention would be the devising of some solution to remove the conditions complained of should I find the complaint was well founded. After my arrival in Dawson on the 14th July, I ascertained that two dance halls respectively culled the M & N and the Florodora were in active operation, and that there was some diversity ot opinion as to whether these institutions weie a menace to public morals or otherwise. My own opinion was that they should be suppressed, and before the session of the Yukon council, which opened on the 9th August last, I had thoroughly canvassed the situation with every member of the Yukon council. I made no secret of the position I proposed to take in the matter. An amendment to the liquor ordinance was introduced by the Hon. Mr. Justice Dugas, providing in effect that no music hall should be kept in connection with premises licensed to sell liquors (section 3, chapter 9 ordinance, 1907). There was some opposition to this Bill in the council, and various amendments proposing the postponement ot the operation of the Bill to a later date received some support, hut eventually the section passed as proposed, the effect being to immediately make the sale of liquors in dance halls illegal. The two dance halls I have mentioned continued to run for some time without selling liquors until the largest, the M & N, went out of business, and the other still continued to run as a dance hall, hut I am credibly informed by the police that there is very little business being done and that no liquors are sold in the dance hall.
The matter then is perfectly plain. Here is the statement of Mr. Pringle that these dance halls, licensed and sanctioned by this government, were no better than dens of iniquity. Here is the report of their own officer, a prominent officer In the Northwest Mounted Police, who makes practically the same statement. Here is the report of Mr. Commissioner Henderson who says that his attention was drawn to this matter by the letter of Mr. Pringle published in a newspaper at Winnipeg, that he looked into the matter and/satisfied himself that Mr. Pringle was right, and that he thereupon canvassed every member of the Yukon council and had the necessary legislation introduced, which was accordingly passed by the council, and which put an end to these public nuisances. That is exactly what I said in the first place and what the Minister of the Interior controverted, and I leave it to the House whether he or I was right.
The next question debated by the minister was whether or not this government were right In practically refusing an investigation into the charges made by Mr. Pringle.
I confess myself unable to follow the devious journeyings of the minister in his argument on this subject. In the first place he said that it was not proper to enter into any investigation of the private conduct or character of public officials. Why then did he propose to grant any Investigation at all ? Why did he authorize Mr. Henderson to make 'any such investigation ? If the private character of public officials, even when It amounts to a public scandal, flaunted in the face-of the whole community, is not a matter of no public interest, why did the Minister of the Interior empower Mr. Henderson to make any investigation into these charges ? Then later on he took the ground that although it was proper to make an inquiry, it was not proper to make one on oath. That does seem to me a most remarkable position for the government to take even through my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior.
You proposed for some reason-the minister did not make it at all clear to grant an inquiry into certain charges made against the conduct of certain government officials and you proposed to refuse the verv thing which alone could make that

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend would take this opportunity to explain on what he bases the supposition that it was of any more importance when it came from the Governor General's office than when it came from the Rev. John Pringle ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Because when it came from Dr. Pringle no action was taken and when it came from the Governor General some action was taken.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon, he is quite in error. Rev. John Pringle wrote to several parties at once. The letter was received in my absence and while I was absent letters were forwarded to my office from the premier and His Excellency. When I arrived I found the letters and I notified Dr. Pringle that I had received his letter and had received the letters from the other parties whom he had notified. They came to me at the same time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We will accept the minister's explanation.
Dear Sir,-I beg to inclose herewith copy oL a letter received by me from the Governor General's office.
Was that letter also addressed to the Minister of the Interior?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I imagine that there was a letter addressed to myself and to the Governor General, that is my remembrance of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The letter to the minister and the communications forwarded to the Prime Minister and the Governor General reached the minister all at the same time?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The minister reached them all at the same time as I remember.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister reached them all at the same time. It is another illustration of my hon. friend's capacity for what he calls the lawyer's quibble. However, I shall read the letter :
Ottawa, August 28, 1907.
Dear Sir,-I beg to inclose herewith copy of a letter received by me from the Governor General's office. As you will note from the address and contents, the original of this letter was addressed to the premier and to my-salf*	11 will be good enough to investigate
fully the specific oharges made by Mr Pringle against Messrs. Girouard and Lith-gow, and you will, of course, call upon Mr Pringle to substantiate those charges. You are to investigate fully and report. Should the Rev. Mr. Pringle desire to lay charges against any other persons in the employ of the government or of the Interior Department especially, you are to investigate them as well.
The minister tells us to-day that he would not issue a Royal commission because the charges were not specific. In his letter of

August 28, 1907, be referred to them as specific charges and they were made much more specific by Dr. Pringle during the negotiations for an investigation which took place between him and Mr. Henderson. So I think that will fairly dispose of the minister's contention that the charges were not specific.
But let us take another authority, if the minister's authority is not sufficient for himself. In a letter from Alexander Henderson, Commissioner, to the Hon. Frank Oliver, Minister of the Interior, bearing date 23rd September, 1907, I find the following statement :
The charge against Mr. Girouard seems to me to be reasonably specific, but I informed Dr. Pringle that before I could hear and investigate charges against Mr. Lithgow, these charges in fairness to Mr. Lithgow should be made definite and specific.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is exactly what you have been saying, aud on October 23, 1907, as will appear on reference to that page, Dr. Pringle, in compliance with the request of the commissioner in that behalf, made his charges against Mr. Lithgow a great deal more specific than those against Mr. Girouard, which already had been declared by the Commissioner to be reasonably specific. So that I think will dispose of the contention of the minister that he did not issue this Royal Commission because the charges were not sufficiently specific.
Why then did the minister refuse to issue a Royal Commission? He had embarked on this investigation after receiving a certain communication from the Governor General's office in connection with the private conduct of certain public officials which was declared to be a public scandal. Let us see how the minister comes out of tlie investigation in that respect. _ The Rev. John Pringle on October 18, 1907, in a letter addressed to the Minister of the Iu-terior, used this language :
When the government appoints an investigator with the power to subpoena, commit and protect witnesses, I shall be ready with overwhelming proof of the truth of the charges I have made.
On the 14th day of October, 1907, in a letter addressed by him to Alexander Hen-, derson, the Commissioner of the Yukon, he said this :
I think, Sir, that the alternatives before you are the following :
1.	As the agent of the Minister of the Interior to inquire into the scandals, at least six years continued, connected with the names of these two officials.
2.	To get from the authorities at Ottawa the
powers of a royal commission to investigate the charge I have made.	.
If you adopt the first course I shall, having made specific charges, do all I can tc aid you
That was the situation. The minister had declared the charges sufficiently specific. Commissioner Henderson had held those against Mr. Girouard to be sufficiently specific, but required further particulars regarding Mr. Lithgow; these particulars were given. Then, Mr. Henderson found himself in a position to proceed, because specific charges against both these men had been filed with him and brought to his attention. Dr. Pringle held, and properly held, that the investigation would be only farcical if there was no power to compel
the attendance of witnesses, to examine those witnesses on oath and to force them ;o speak. So, in the letter I have read, the commissioner, Mr. Henderson, suggested that he should be given power to make the investigation an effective one. And the only answer of the minister is that he saw fit to differ from Mr. Henderson in that opinion, and, for that reason, he refused any effective investigation; that is the best I can make out of it. The minister is in this dilemma : charges had been made of a character which were a public scandal, so that a public servant of this country, if the charges were true, should no longer hold his office. In that case there should be an investigation-an effective, and not a farcical investigation. If, on the other hand, the charges were not of a character to affect the status of a public servant, there should not have been any investigation at all either informal or effective. The minister started the informal investigation, not only acknowledging that the charges were of a character to affect the status of a pub-lie servant, but that those charges were sufficiently specific, and they more specific afterwards-but, when the true situation was placed beore him, for some reason not made known to this House, he declined absolutely to allow witnesses to be examined on oath and rendeied

abortive any attempt on the part of Dr. Pringle to prove that the charges were true. In the result, that is unfair to the public servants themselves-there can be no question about that. Because, Di\ Pringle, having the courage of his convictions, has not been silent during the last four or five years : on the public platform and in the press he has made known to the people of the Yukon and of Canada generally the charges that he has asked the minister to investigate. When this government, acting through its Minister of the Interior, declined to investigate these charges in any effective way, they did a grievous injustice not only to the people of this country but to those two men as well. More than that, they did an injury to the public service of the country, and they have shaken public confidence in the intention of the government to carry on as it ought to be carried on the government of the Yukon. So far as Mr. Lithgow and Mr. Girouard are concerned, I pass no opinion as to the truth of the charges against them; no member of this House is called upon to do that. What we insist upon is that, charges having been made and investigation ordered, and these charges touching the value of the service of these gentlemen as public servants, there should be a proper investigation. So far as integrity as a public servant is concerned, and so far as capacity is concerned, ail I knew of Mr. Lithgow when he was in Halifax many years ago, in the public service there, led me to believe that he would be a valuable public servant in the Yukon. I have no knowledge of his conduct in the Yukon, and no knowledge concerning Mr. Girouard ; but I do believe that these charges ought to have been investigated, and ought to have been investigated in an effectual way. In the result the minister lias seen fit to leave upon the records of this country, in the shape of the affidavits forwarded by Dr. Pringle in regard to Mr Girouard in 1905, and upon the records of parliament sworn testimony which Mr. Gironar^l, as well as the government, ought to have desired to have investigated and investigated to the utmost. If the charges against Mr. Giourard are false, then the men who made these affidavits and the men who put forward these charges ought not to be walking the streets of this country in perfect immunity. On the other hand, if the statements in these affidavits are correct as to the conduct of Mr. Girouard on a certain occasion, then the government of this country is sadly in default in having permitted him, for the past four years, to exercise the functions of a public servant in the Yukon. There is the dilemma ; you can take either one horn or the other, as you see fit. It is the result of the inaction of this government ; for, the very moment that these affidavits were placed on the Mr. R. ju BORDEN.
files of the Department of the Interior, it was the duty of the government, without regard to Dr. Pringle or anybody else, to have the mattter probed to the bottom. The minister (Mr. Oliver) seems to think this is purely a matter between Mr. Pringle and the government, and that if he (Mr. Oliver) can discredit Dr. Pringle in some way, if he can cast some aspersion upon his character or conduct or motive, he has disposed of the question. But it is a much larger question than that; it is a question of public morals in the Yukon; it is a question of the administration of public affairs in a distant portion of the country. The issue, to my mind, is scarcely such as the Minister of the Interior would suggest. I regret that the government have seen fit to adopt the course they have adopted. It will not be commended by any intelligent citizen in this country, Liberal or Conservative, who really understands the facts and the situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As the letters of Dr. Pringle, which have been made the subject of this debate, were addressed not only to the Department of the Interior, but also to myself-and, indeed, for that matter, to the whole of the cabinet-perhaps it would not be out of place for me to give my views on this question as it arose from time to time from 1902 up to the present year. Addressing myself at this moment to my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), who has taken charge of this matter and who has read the correspondence out and out, I may say to him that, as I saw that correspondence as it arose from time to time, beginning in 1902, added to in 1905 and added to still further in 1907, it seemed to me that these letters came from a gentleman who certainly was zealous for the public weal, but one whose discretion and language, perhaps, were not such as to strike one very favourably. I cannot help having for Dr. Pringle great respect, for certainly, he has shown that he is very much in earnest in prosecuting what he considered to be the public good. At the same time, for my part, I might have wished that his language was a little more moderate than it always was in his communications. My hon. friend has read numerous letters which have been addressed to the government by Dr. Pringle, but he read only one part of the letter of 1902.
I read the whole of the 1905 letters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my hon. friend did not read the whole, but only part.
I read probably nine-tenths. There is here and there a little passage that I did not read.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Exactly, my hon. friend left out several passages which

I think he did very well to leave out. But, in that letter of 1902 there was nothing that he could not place upon the pages of ' Hansard ' and allow it to go to the country. I have to observe to my hon. friend that in this letter of 1902 there is nothing definite, there is nothing positive, but it is full of general assertions, assertions of immorality in certain quarters, assertions of malfeasance in other quarters, assertions of peculations and other offences in still other quarters. My hon. friend expressed some doubt as to the propriety of the course which was followed on that occasion by the government. He expressed surprise that no action had been taken. The reason, Mr. Speaker, seems to be very obvious. I ask my hon. friend what action could have been taken by the government upon a letter of the character of the one that we are now discussing ; that is the letter of 1902 ? I repeat, no name is mentioned, officials are aspersed with some vehemence but no names given, charges are made of a very indefinite character which could not be investigated.
