But at that moment, when Mr. Pringle was addressing the government and making complaints as to what was going on in the Yukon, or at a later date, if not at that moment, the Yukon was presided over by Mr. Ross and to the efforts of Mr Ross he gave the most ample credit. Not only does he give credit to his efforts but he also gives credit to Mr. Ross for the success of his efforts and he says, in so many words, in the correspondence, that Mr. Ross, during his administration, had succeeded in uprooting many of the evils of which he had been complaining. Unfortunately, the administration of Mr. Ross was not very long, not as long as perhaps it should have been for the good of the Yukon. The difficulty which the government has always had in the Yukon has been to get such ofiicials as would discharge their duties in a manner that would be satisfactory to all concerned. As my hon. friend has said, the Yukon is a land of mystery. It is so far off that I think my hon. friend will agree that it is difficult, with the numerous officials that the government has to employ there to make sure that every one of these persons shall be of the character which we would all desire. Mr. Ross was an exceptional man, he was a most successful administrator and everybody bears testimony to that fact, not only his friends but his opponents, every man who has had any thing to do with the Yukon bears testimony that under Mr. Ross, as also under the administration of Mr. Henderson, his successor, the Yukon was and is well administered. But, with Mr. Ross' departure the complaints commenced again. The character of the administration established by Mr. Ross is
well justified by tbe correspondence of Mr. Pringle himself because, Mr. Pringle who, as I said a moment ago, I think, was actuated by a desire for the public weal, allowed three years to elapse before addressing any further complaint to the government. He addressed his first complaint to the government during the administration of Mr. Ross in the year 1902. In the month of January, 1905, Mr. Pringle sent another complaint. Communication is reasonably speedy when navigation is open, but as soon as navigation is closed communication is very slow. I do not remember the exact time at which the letter reached me but I am quite sure that when the letter reached me the hon. gentleman who had been Minister of the Interior was no more in office. That hon. gentleman resigned about the commencement of March and it was about that time I received the letter from Mr. Pringle. In that letter of Mr. Pringle there were two charges ; charges were made against two different parties, Mr. Congdon and Mr. Girouard especially. The charge against Mr. Girouard was a very positive, specific character. It was not so much a charge of a direct offence committed by him but it was leading to a very direct charge against him. The matter dropped at that time because there was an interregnum in the Department of the Interior, but in the summer of that year the new Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) who wanted to know exactly what the condition was in the Yukons took the very wise precaution of proceeding to the Yukon himself so as to investiagte all matters and see what was to be done. We know that the result of his trip has been very far reaching and that it has corrected many abuses of which the people complained and has introduced a new era into the administration of that country. As I understood from my hon. friend on his return, he heard no complaints whatever from anybody of the character which have been mentioned in Mr. Pringle's letter of January, 1905. But, more than that, the letter of Mr. Pringle was referred, by the Minister of Justice, who had received also similar complaints from Mr. Pringle, to Mr. Congdon for his observations upon it and Mr. Congdon denied absolutely all the allegations of fact contained in Mr. Pringle's letter. This disposes of the charges made by Mr. Pringle in 1905.
But the latter charge which was brought by Mr. Pringle in 1907 was perhaps the most important of all and it was one to which immediate attention had to be given. Mr. Pringle, in his letter of 1907, made positive accusations against two officials of the government in the Yukon. I think Mr Girouard and Mr. Lithgow, who were the parties charged by Mr. Pringle, are

acknowledged to have been very good officers discharging the duties of their offices remarkably well. Of Mr. Lithgow, especially, I am bound to say, in justice to him, that there is not in the Yukon a more painstaking officer or one who commands more generally the respect of the community than he does. Everybody acknowledges that. I do not know Mr. Lithgow personally, I do not remember of ever having seen him, but in all of the correspondence I have had about him' testimony is rendered universally to the fact that he is a most competent officer and discharges his duty fairly well. But, he is of the human race and he is not free from faults. He has his faults, I am bound to say, but with the faults he has. everybody in the Yukon, while acknowledging his faults, will say at the same time that he is a good, competent officer. This is the testimony which I have to bear of him and which I think is only his due. The charges that were made by Mr. Pringle against Mr. Girouard were very formal. They could not be ignored. What was to be done under such circumstances ? I appeal again to my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Poster) : What would he have done under such circumstances ? He was a minister at one time, and he had numerous officers under him. Let us take a hypothetical case. If the hon. member for North Toronto had been in office and if some one had made the charge against any of his officers that he had been guilty of intoxication, not only privately but openly in the streets of the city, what would he have done ? Would the hon. gentleman have appointed a royal commission to investigate the charge and pronounce upon it ? The offence is a private one but it may be such that a minister may have to take notice of it, and sometimes a minister does. In my humble opinion this was a case Ifor departmental investigation by the minister to ascertain whether the official was guilty, and if guilty whether he was excusable or whether he should be expelled from the service. I am glad to say these things do not occur very often, but they do happen almost every year in the public service and the minister in charge of the department concerned does not appoint a royal commission under the great seal of His Majesty to investigate such cases. It is a departmental affair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is a provision for a departmental investigation under. oath.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think that the investigation of such an offence would come under chapter 104 respecting public and departmental inquiries, which says :

The minister presiding over any department of the civil service of Canada may appoint at any time under authority of the Governor in Council a commissioner or commissioners to investigate and report upon the state and management of the business or any part of the business of such department, either the inside or outside service thereof, and the conduct of any person in such service so far as the same relates to his official duties.
My hon. friend is a good lawyer and I think he will agree with me that the charge made by Mr. Pringle did not come under the scope of that Act. However, I will not examine this case in the light of the technicalities of tlie law but rather under the broader law of common sense, common fair play, and common justice to the accuser and to the accused. Under such circumstances I say that the action taken by the minister was very proper. Had these officials resided in Ottawa the minister himself might have decided what should be done, but in this case he had to delegate his power and he gave instructions to Mr. Henderson to look into the matter and to ask Mr. Prlncle to attend and investigate the charges. Mr. Pringle was notified, but he said he would uot come to the investigation unless lie had a royal commission to compel the attendance of witnesses and to have the protection of the law for them. Now, the charge made by Mr. Pringle was that these officials had been guilty of public scandal in their private conduct, and lie said it was notorious and that the whole community of Yukon bad been aware of it. Was it not the duty of Mr. Priugle when the commissioner was authorized to receive liis complaint, to come before the commissioner and to say that he made these charges for such and such a reason seeing that he bad alleged they were notorious and a public scandal? Then, when Mr. Pringle would not come forward Mr. Henderson investigated for his own satisfaction the life of these officials.
In what manner did Mr. Henderson make any investigation as reported by him ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I don't mean to say that Mr. Henderson pried into the private life of these gentlemen or that he examined any witnesses to burrow into their lives to see whether they had misbehaved themselves or not. But the commissioner dealt with the charge of Mr. Pringle as couched in this letter, that these men had behaved in their private life in a public and scandalous manner. The commissioner was able to say to the minister : I live in Dawson ; I have been here for some time ; I know these men ; I know they are good officials and discharge their duties properly, I have not heard of any such public scandals as are mentioned by Mr. Pringle.
He says : Since I came here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is the substance of the report he made to the minister. Mr. Henderson has been in the Yukon since May, 1907 and Mr. Pringle's letter was written in July, 1907, and here is part of the letter which I can read.
The disgraceful scenes of the last ten days in which prominent public men and government officials of more than one department have been the chief aotoTS, have more than justified everything I have written to members of the cabinet or to the press in regard to the immorality which prevails in our community and official life.
What is the date of that ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is the very last charge made by Mr. Pringle on tbe 27tii of July, 1907. With this language of Mr. Pringle before him the commissioner reports to the minister : I am not aware that anything lias taken place in the life of these men which I can report on ; I know them to he good and honourable men. That is the comment of the commissioner. Mr. Pringle would not come before the comiriissioner and I think lie was not fair to himself in that. I repeat the minister was perfectly right in refusing at that time to issue a commission under the King's great seal to investigate the private conduct of these two officials. The minister was told he had two men in his service who had misbehaved in a public and scandalous manner in the community. If they were guilty of such scandal he would probably come to the conclusion they were not fit to remain in the service, or at all events he would call upon them to give their explanation of theiv excuse as to whether or not they should be retained in the service. Therefore it was open to Mr. Pringle to come forward with his evidence, his own and that of other witnesses before the commissioner. If the other witnesses had refused to come forward, the commissioner could have reported tlie fact to the minister, and have advised a further investigation. But in the circumstances of the case, I say that the conduct of the Minister of the Interior was absolutely right. Certainly it was not his duty to order such a solemn proceeding as an investigation by a royal commission into matters which were departmental, affecting the private conduct of officials.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the charges had been proved would they have justified dismissal ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the charges had been proved with regard to one of the officers I would say yes, they would. But let us take a supposititious case. Suppose it were true that Mr. Lithgow had misbe-liaved on a certain occasion; suppose he had been intoxicated, I would say for my part to the minister :	Give that man a further
chance; do not dismiss him; he is a good officer ; I would not be thet first one to cast
a stone at him ; he may have misbehaved, but he is doing better and will do better, and I would not dismiss him. That would be my advice to the minister. But it is a very different thing for a man to be accused of having continuously lived in open shame to the scandal of the community.
I have no hesitation in saying that such a man would have to make a very strong case before I would retain him in the service. But if such a good officer as Mr. Lithgow has the misfortune to make a break, as the saying is, I would ask him to give his promise that he would not fall again, and on that condition I would not dismiss him from the service. I repeat, I do not know Mr. Lithgow, I never saw him, but all the reports that I have had from the Yukon agree that his public conduct has been remarkably good and in the public interest. That is my own view of tlie matter. I may say further that I know -and perhaps my hon. friend from North Toronto knows also-that there are men of the same persuasion and I think of the same cloth as Mr. Pringle who do not take the view he does with regard to Mr. Lithgow. After all, in a country like the Yukon, if a man has the misfortune, as we say in common parlance, to make a break,
I think it would not he wise on the part of the government to exact frprn him the pound of flesh and be absolutely merciless towards him.
With regard to Mr. Girouard, who has been accused of the most grievous offence, he could not remain in the service with that cloud over his head. He had to do one of two things, and he has done both. First of all, he had to clear his character, and to do that he brought an action for libel against Mr. Pringle, which action I understand is pending. I was asked by an hon. member if the action had been tried. As I understand, the courts in the Yukon take their recess during the winter and sit during the summer, so that the case has not yet been tried. At all events, Mr. Girouard has left the service, and, therefore, these matters are not perhaps of much interest at the present time except so far as they show whether or not the government have done their duty. I have only to repeat that, in my humble judgment, the minister in this matter behaved as he should have behaved ; he gave Mr. Pringle the opportunity to bring his charges and have them investigated, and Mr. Pringle was not fair to himself when he refused that opportunity. If he had taken it, and if the witnesses on whom he relied had not come forward, then it would have been oi>en to the minister to decide whether or not he would prosecute any further. The House will agree with me that the minister did his full duty, not only to Mr. Pringle, but to himself and to the government of which he is a member.
At six o'clock, House took recess.

After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

I wish to deal somewhat briefly with the subject at present engaging our attention. That subject is the alleged misconduct of officials in the Yukon Territory extending oyer a period of six years. From time to time charges of misconduct on the part of these officials were made to the government- charges of misconduct, of immorality, of dishonesty, of graft-and in various ways it was brought to the attention of the government that the officials in that remote territory were not conducting themselves in a manner creditable to the administration or the country. These charges date from the year 1882, and two of the officials especially implicated were Messrs. Lith-gow and Girouard. The charges were first made by the Rev. John Pringle in 1902. Mr. Pringle speaking of the conditions prevalent in the Yukon among government officials, stated that the characteristic of these officials were ' lust and graft,' and claimed that no one was able to secure what rightly belonged to him unless he were 'on the inside' and ' had a pull.' In other words, it was impossible for those who were prosecuting the industry of mining to either secure ,or maintain their rights without influence at court, and that influence was presumably an improper one. In a public meeting jn Dawson City, it was stated publicly, before an audience of hundreds of people, that such concessions as the ' Bronson and Ray,' and the ' Philp ' concessions, granted on representations which were, to say the least, suggestive of perjury. Mr. Pringle says that he heard it said that two cabinet ministers were in these. In case I might be charged with misquoting, let me give the exact words used : I
I heard it stated before an audience of hundreds by a lawyer named Woodworth that two cabinet .ministers, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Siffon) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine) were interested in one or more of these loosely granted concessions.
Now, if Mr. Woodworth was making a statement which was libellous, you would naturally expect that he would be prosecuted, because the statement was of too important a character to he allowed to pass Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
unnoticed. If he were not making a libellous statement, then tbe government were remiss in their duty iu not calling them to account for it.
Hear, bear.
I should like to know what it Is that so much amuses tbe bon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). Is it laughable that any minister of tbe gospel should make such a charge ?
He is amused at the word ' lle-bellious '.

What does tbe bon. gentleman know about it ? Nothing more than to sit and laugh. We know the saying that laughter at times denotes the vacant mind, and that is evidently the case in this instance, because the bon. gentleman appears Deither willing to take tbe trouble to inquire into tile facts nor desirous of knowing them. Instead he treats the whole thing with levity, though it is the solemn statement of a minister of the gospel who, in his desire to improve the morals of the people, brought the matter to the attention of the ministers of the Crown so that they might have it inquired into and, punish those guilty of corrupt acts if the charges were established. If the charges were libellous, the party who made them could be punished, and surely no minister of the Crown- especially those implicated-could afford to let them pass unheeded. Mr. Pringle specially stated that the Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries were specially interested in one or more of those loosely granted concessions. I draw more particularly attention to this because of the statement made by the right hon. first minister to-night that he saw nothing In these charges which ought to engage his attention. There was nothing in them, he said, to warrant an inquiry. They were all of a general character and there was not a single specific allegation. But was uot the public declaration made before a large audience that two of the right hou. gentleman's colleagues are improperly interested in Certain concessions sufficiently specific. Yet the first minister himself said : I see nothing in these charges upon which to hinge an inquiry. They are of such a vague and general character that there Is nothing to inquire Into. Yet this man says that two cabinet ministers, the Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Marine, were interested In one or snore of these loosely granted concessions.
Then he says :
Concessions have been granted, I am convinced, not only carelessly but iniquitously ; the heritage of our people given to satisfy the greed of capital, without due consideration of the rights of the people in the ground or of the character of the statements made to secure these concessions.

He charges general immorality, but yet the First Minister says these charges are vague and general and there is nothing to inquire into. IVhat does he say?
The dance halls in which more men, some of them government officials, have been ruined than in any other of our protected dens, are run wide open. I wish the government would, for its own good name, either suppress these ' hells,' or at least take means to verify reports

But there is nothing there to inquire into

-current all over this camp, about officials who are their habitues. Prostitution flaunts itself everywhere, the abandoned woman, (to say nothing of the abandoned man) is everywhere ; beside respectable homes ; across the street from then; beside our grocery and dry goods stores; on first and second and third, and every avenue and road. Unless some one is robbed or injured in her house she is undisturbed.
He goes on to say :
But the worst feature of the licensed houses here is, that a very large percentage of them are houses of prostitution.
He tells us that there were 210 houses licensed to sell liquor there at that time and yet there was a population of, at the most, 20,000 people, That is about one licensed house for every 95 of the population in that district.
But the worst feature of the licensed houses here is, that a very large percentage of them are houses of prostitution. Many of them run, it is true, by people of good character but a large number are bawdy houses with a government license to prey upon the public.
And yet the government are not concerned about it and see nothing to inquire into.
I have wondered since coming north, why the permit system was adopted. Was it to restrict the sale of liquor ?
At the time it was adopted we were told it was in the interest of temperance. I remember the ex-minister saying that this was one of the means we kept in our own hands for the purpose of promoting temperance in these camps in the west.
I have wondered since coming north, w-hy the permit system was adopted. Was it to restrict the sale of liquor or to make it respectable or to make money for government exigencies, or to make money for men with a pull?
I think the experience of times since has proven one thing, that it made money for men with a pull. We remember when J. D. McGregor, the license inspector there who had authority to give permits, refused permits to a number of people who desired them to take liquor into that country, but gave it to be understood to one of his friends that a permit would be granted to him. That man rushed in all his liquor in
the fall of the year when navigation was expected shortly to close and then the permit was granted when it was too late for others to bring liquor in. McGregor then resigned his position as inspector and became a member of the firm that got the permit. I believe he was one of three who shared in the profits and I am told they made a large amount of money. With these facts before us, can we say that the permit system was intended to restrict the sale of liquor? No, it was rather to make money for government exigencies or to make money for men with a pull. He was one of the men with a pull.
Rev. Mr. Pringle says:
The law is systematically manipulated not to protect the public, but to protect and nurse the gambler and shame honest men.
This man speaks with knowledge and has been very reasonable and fair in the statements he has made. Speaking of the Northwest Mounted Police he says that they are a splendid body of men, the finest on the earth but:
It is enough to degrade any force, however fine, to know that where immorality is concerned it is useless to do their duty, that the law itself will be made to thwart them and defeat the ends of justice when they endeavour to carry it out.
I have written in plain terms because if I am asked what right I have to so address the government of Canada I answer that I am a Canadian and love my native land. I hold that we have a right to expect that the men who represent our government, the officers of the law and the departments of the country should not only do justly but live rightly. I have said publicly here and I repeat it that there is a conscience in the west and I shall do my best to arouse and invoke that conscience and I shall refuse to be silenced as long as this continues.
Mr. Pringle follows this up by affidavits which are here from different parties setting forth the crookedness of the officials there with regard to their conduct in political life, and speaks of one of the commissioners who is absolutely keeping the list from the people while he is known to be in a house of prostitution. X have affidavits here presumably from respectable people.

speechtext: I think my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) must have taken down my words incorrectly. I do not recall having alleged that the Rev. John Pringle, in making his charges, had a political purpose. If I did I certainly did not intend to.

That is the inference I drew. If I misunderstood the hon. gentleman I wish to withdraw my statement because I do not desire to misrepresent him in any particular. But, if he did not do it I find that some others have. I have here a copy of the ' Daily News-Advertiser ' of Vancouver, B.C., and I notice that a writer in that draws attention to it. It reads as follows:
To the editor ' News-Advertiser.'
Sir,-I noticed in a recent issue of the Vancouver ' Province,' an interview given by Mr. Alexander Henderson, commissioner of the Yukon

He says that Rev. John Pringle is doing it for some other purpose rather than for the purpose of elevating the moral standard of the people.
-lately from Dawson, headed ' Pringle campaign a political one.' 'It is a political move '
My hon. friend is not quoting the commissioner's interview. My hon. friend is quoting a letter.
I am quoting a letter stating what the commissioner said.
No, my hon. friend is not.
I am.
The interview was not given to the ' News-Advertiser.' The interview was given to the ' Province.'
I am quoting a letter written to the ' News-Advertiser.'
Yes, but I want my hon. friend to make the distinction fairly.
Have I not made it fairly? Have I not said that it was a letter written to this paper? Is that not fair enough? How much fairer could it be? It is impossible to make it any fairer.

My hon. friend purports to give a statement made by Governor Henderson that Rev. .John Pringle was conducting a political campaign. If my hon. friend will be fair he will quote Governor Henderson's interview, not a letter written by some one else referring to that interview.

Am I not reading this letter ? If the hon. gentleman will listen a little more attentively he will find out that he was mistaken in his observations. What does this say?
I noticed in a recent issue of the Vancouver ' Province ' an interview given by Mr. Alexander Henderson.
Am I stating other than facts?
That is all right.
Well, then, why get up and interrupt ?
I have a reason for interrupting. The reason I interrupted was that my hon. friend purports to use a statement of Governor Henderson when, as a matter of fact, he has not the interview before him.

I do not purport to use any statement at all. I purport to read a letter, let it carry whatever weight it will in the House, and that letter sets forth that this is an interview given by Governor Henderson. The letter says :
I noticed in a recent issue of the Vaneou-ver ' Province ' an interview given by Mr. Alex. Henderson, commissioner of the Yukon lately from Dawson, headed ' Pringle Campaign a 'political one.' ' It is a political move,' started off the commissioner, in discussing the recent allegation of Rev. John Pringle, concerning the immorality of Dawson.
* He intends taking the stump.' ' He has fallen out with the government and will take the field in the Conservative interest, that is the explanation, I think'; 'the dance halls have been closed, and will not be re-opened.
Knowing what I am writing, for, I may say, I have lived several years in Dawson, and have fairly well kept tabs on matters there, going back half a dozen years, I will begin with the dance halls, which were authorized and made legal institutions during the Congdon regime, largely through the instrumentality of the appointed members of the Yukon Council, including Mr. J. E. Girouard, who also stood firmly by the dance hall element at the time they were put out of business, and during the present commissioner's time. As to the immorality of Dawson, to any one who knows and has kept the run of the matters, when any of the government advocates, from the commissioner down to Pinkert, assail Mr. Pringle as having said that Dawson is immoral, they are trying the old dodge of the herring across the trail. Mr. Pringle has in public print denied this charge, and has said that the opposite is the case. He has stated that certain of the government office holders have been leading such lives as to disgrace them and their offices. He Mr. SPROULE.
has oamimunicatted this to the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior on several occasions, mostly without any effect.
Recently these matters have caused some folks to ' sit up and take notice,' and the outcome is that an action for damages has been instituted against Mr. Pringle (not by the city of Dawson, but by the friend of the dance halls). We see in the Dawson ' Daily News ' of April 10, 1908, in extenso statements of claim and defence in the libel suit of J. E. Girouard vs. Rev. John Pringle. As most of the subject matter would he almost considered: ancient and true history to Dawsonites, it would not likely be any surprise to them but to one so new to the territory as Commissioner Henderson, one would expect it would give him some concern, especially as it involved one whose services in the Yukon council he had ' found invaluable and had learned to lean on him.'
One is more than surprised to see in the April l#h issue of the same * Daily News ' that a farewell banquet is given to this same J. E. Girouard, at which Commissioner Henderson in his speech ' predicted from what he had learned that Mr. Girouard would he given an opportunity of a seat in parliament.' ' Mr. Henderson rose to enthusiastic and dramatic fervour during his talk,' says the ' News.' In the Dawson ' Daily News ' of April 15, 1908, is a list of the ' guests,' beginning with Commissioner Henderson and former Commissioner F. T. Congdon and a long list of others, a few of whom would hardly he expected to be found at a banquet given to a party accused of sheep stealing which would be a very trivial offence against society compared with the matters mentioned in the Dawson ' Daily News ' of April 10 last. But every one to their taste. When Commissioner Henderson says of Mr. Pringle's action. ' lit is a political move,' he would seem to be measuring other people's corn by bis own half bushel.'
Now as to this J. Girouard we were told by the Minister of the Interior to-day that he is no longer in the employ of the government and that he has gone God knows where. I imagine his suit against the Rev. John Pringle will not be prosecuted further. It would seem from this letter I have read that some one accuses the Rev. John Pringle of having nothing but a political aim in view, and Henderson the present commissioner goes to a complimentary banquet given to this man who is practically an outlaw of society, to try and make him somewhat respectable. And yet the Minister of the Interior sees nothing wrong in it. It is a nice position for the commissioner of the Yukon. What will the world think of it when they know this.

Know what ?
. IMr. SPROULE. Know that the present commissioner to the Yukon attended a banquet to such a man and made use of the remarks he did and vilified the Rev. John Pringle because he was honest and independent and truthful enough to say what he believed to be true.
Who vilified the Rev. John Pringle ?
I say that as far as I know Mr. Henderson did so when he said that the Rev. Mr. Pringle took this action for political purposes. If that is not vilification, what is it ?
The hon. gentleman takes a letter written by a man in Vancouver and a letter from Dawson and compounds the two and reads that.

Not at all. What is contained in that letter is what is stated by Mr. Henderson.
take his word as readily as the word of the Rev. John Pringle? Did you ever yet see a prisoner at the bar who did not plead not guilty? Mr. Congdon's denial is a plea of not guilty, but these affidavits which I have read from seven or eight individuals swear to something different. Will you give as much credence to the denial of interested parties, who are charged before the bar of public opinion, as you will to the statements of a disinterested party who swears to what he knows to be facts?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that the Rev. Dr. Pringle has sworn to any facts? He had an opportunity to do so.

If my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Macpherson) will get the Dawson ' News ' of April 14, he will find in it a three-column report of the banquet with Mr. Henderson's statement, and the extracts my hon. friend has read have been evidently taken from that paper.
My hon. friend from North Toronto does not bear out then what the hon. member for East Grey states.
Yes, because one part of Mr. Henderson's speech is the allegation that Mr. Pringle's motive was a political motive.
The interview is given in the ' Progress ' and the letter my hon. friend reads is from the ' Progress.'

What my hon. friend is reading from is a letter written to the [DOT] News-Advertiser ' by * Bona Fide,' and dated Vancouver, May 12, 1908, and he gives a quotation from the Dawson 'Daily News ' of April 14.
And the interview with Commissioner Henderson.
My hon. friend gives Commissioner Henderson's words as contained in that interview. Therefore, it is direct enough, and it ought to be correct.
Why does not the hon. gentleman read the interview?
I read the interview, which was in that letter between inverted commas, and so far as I know it has never been contradicted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If there is a clash of evidence between the Rev. Dr. Pringle and Commissioner Henderson, why is not the word of Commissioner Henderson as good as that of Rev. Dr. Pringle?
Because the one is an interested party and the other is not.
Which one?
The Commissioner is the interested party, because he is defending himself. The First Minister says that Mr. Girouard has denied it; should we not

I have said that the Rev. John Pringle and others have made certain charges and these charges are backed up by affidavits. The First Minister says that we should accept the denial of Mr. Girouard and be perfectly satisfied with that against the sworn statements of seven or eight people as to what they saw with their own eyes. The First Minister and the Minister of the Interior desire to go no further, but turn round and practically insinuate untruthfulness on the part of the Rev. John Pringle without giving him the proper opportunity to prove his charges. I say that the country will_ not be satisfied with that. The First Minister says they gave him an opportunity, but they wanted to have his charges as specific as a charge made against a man charged with crime before a magistrate. They refused to- allow Dr. Pringle to subpoena the witnesses and bring them before the court to prove his charges. They tell him to go and ask the witnesses to come, and in the meantime in all human probability the government officials would buy them off or spirit them away. There are strong grounds for believing that would be done, because the Rev. John Pringle says the administration of justice in that country is practically a farce-that instead of the Mounted Police being permitted to enforce the law, the law is invoked to prevent them enforcing it. In the province of Ontario we have found time and again, both during the Ross administration and the Mowat administration preceding it, that people could not be convicted of political crimes, because the' moment the charges were made against them the witnesses were bought off or spirited away and kept in the United States. So it is in the Yukon. The administration is in the hands of men who do not desire to administer justice, but desire to prevent the administration of justice, and the same thing would most likely have happened if the Rev. John Pringle had attempted to prove his charges m the way proposed by the First Minister. But the Rev. Dr. Pringle said:	Do as you do
before any committee of the House! of Commons; subpoena these people in the



regular way, and then if they refuse or neglect to come, they can be dealt with for contempt of court, and when you bring them to the bar, put them under oath, so that they will tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.
But the Minister of the Interior said : I shall not give you the advantage of subpoenaing them. You can ask them to come; and if they do not, it is not my fault. I have given you the opportunity to prove your charges, and it is for you to prove them without any aid from me. Is that how a man should be treated who made these charges for the sole purpose of letting his party know what was bringing them into contempt and purging the political life of his country of what was bound, if unchecked, to demoralize it ? Will the country be satisfied with this failure to prosecute ? I ,very much misjudge the character of our people if they will. We have been told over and over again that the administration of justice in that country was vicious. We have been told that by parties who live out there and in whose integrity I have every confidence, and judging by the shuffling and evasive conduct of the government I have no doubt that every word they said is true. Mr. Pringle was perfectly justified in refusing to go on with the inquiry unless it was conducted on proper lines and unless he were given a fair opportunity to prove his charges. Was he given that ? Not at all. Yet the Minister of the Interior says there was nothing to inquire into. He takes the ground that the moral character of the government officials was not a subject for inquiry at all, that it was a matter in which the government had no interest. No doubt my hon. friend is sincere on that contention judging by the fact that although Wagner had been twice prosecuted and had been sentenced by the court and compelled to suffer the penalty due his offences, he was afterwards taken up by the minister and put into a responsible position. That evidently is the minister's idea of the right kind of a man to act as government official. Wherever the hon. gentleman got his training, he is evidently sincere, but I wonder what the great honest public, what the moral and church going element of our community, what the ministers of the Gospel will think when they find that doctrine propagated by a minister of the Crown' In my judgment, they will form a very low estimate of the morale of the Minister of the Interior. That however is the position he takes, and the responsibility for that position is with the government. Sooner or later their misdeeds will recoil upon them. When they appeal to the country,
I have no doubt that thousands of honest, good meaning reformers will refuse to de-

clare by their ballots that the government did their duty when they did not carry out this investigation. They will refuse to endorse the conduct of the Minister of the Interior and the Prime Minister and will show by their vote that they consider them anything but men of the highest type of character and animated by the best intentions.

I shal endeavour to be as brief as possible as I do not wish to assist my hon. friends opposite in their obstruction or play into their hands any longer than the necessity of the case requires. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition was careful, in replying to the Minister of the Interior to indulge in his usual introduction by saying that the speech he had just listened to from that hon. Minister was one of the most * extraordinary ' he had ever heard.
He only uses that when the Minister of the Interior speaks.

I notice that when he answers the right hon. the First Minister, whose speech has taken the wind out of the leader of the opposition, my hon. friend was wont to say that the speech he has just heard is the most ' remarkable ' one he ever listened to.
That seldom happens.

My hon. friend will find it frequently happens. It is a most convenient form of reply when one has no effective argument to make, and I have no doubt we will find it frequently resorted to before this session is through. Our hon. friends opposite have not had much success in their attack on the administration of this government in the Yukon. Their main attack was on the proposition of the government to build a railway to the Yukon. On that question, although they presented something of a united front, when we have had some light thrown on the inside facts, as we have had by one of the principal members of the opposition sitting very close to the leader of that party, learn that they were not so united as they led the country to believe they were. We have had the statement from Sir Charles Tupper, who is a true Canadian, that two great mistakes were committed by the Conservative party. One was a trivial mistake and the other was a serious one, namely, their opposition to the proposition of the government to build a railwav to the Yukon.
If my hon. friend had read the papers, he would have seen an explicit denial by Sir Charles Tupper of that statement.
I have not seen it. I have been away for several days and possibly missed the paper which gave publicity to it.
It was in the ' Vancouver News Advertiser'

I have not seen it; and since we have not heard from the hon. member from Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Sam. Hughes), I do not think that he could have seen it either or we would have had him on his feet on another question of privilege. However, we will let that rest. I desire to say nothing but what is fair, but the country will have its own idea of the policy of the opposition when it attacked the Yukon railway proposition and will have its own idea as to whether or not there may not after all be a grain of truth in the statement of the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Sam. Hughes). With all due respect to the great ability of Sir Charles Tupper, it is just possible that his memory may be at fault and that, without any reflection on his desire to be accurate, he may not have fully recollected the facts, and that there was consequently some truth in the straight statement which we had from the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Sam. Hughes). Coming more particularly to the proposition before us, we find that the only sources for the attacks of hon. gentlemen opposite regarding the administration of the Yukon are a certain young men's club in Dawson city and the Revd. Mr. Pringle. Mr. Pringle has been in public life many years, and it is no injustice to say of him that he has been almost always a man with a grievance. Whether federal matters or territorial matters were in question, he has always had an eye for a grievance. The statement was made this afternoon, and we find it in the letter of Mr. Pringle himself, that he is not in politics. Well, while I do not wish to impugn the honesty of the reverend gentleman, I must say that I do not see how that can be, because in the whole history of the Yukon territory there has been no man out there who has been more intensely and constantly active in political life. To such an extent has that been the case that I know of no one who has had so many intense friends and so many bitter enemies as he had while in the Yukon council. The result was that he ceased to be a member of that council, and had he run again, he would have had no show of being re-elected. I wish it to be understood that I have no reflection to make on Mr. Pringle personally. I do not desire to express any opinion concerning him, but we have his own statements, all made in a spirit of the greatest bitterness, against Mr. Congdon
307i
who won the nomination at the last election. Although in many respects Mr. Pringle is eminently fitted for public life yet the Liberal convention did not think so and in their wisdom they selected Mr. Congdon. And from that day to this, although previously he and Mr. Congdon were good friends, he became Mr. Congdon's determined enemy. It was stated by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that Mr. Henderson compromised himself by attending a banquet given to Mr. Congdon. Why, Mr. Pringle himself attended a banquet given to Mr. Congdon before Mr. Congdon secured the nomination to this House. When Mr. Congdon was appointed commissioner, the citizens of Dawson gave him a banquet and one of those who raised their voices most favourably in praise of Mr. Congdon was Mr. Pringle himself. But afterwards they became estranged, there occurred this cleavage between them and we find the condition which exists to-day where there seems to be a spirit of the utmost revenge, not to use a stronger word, in the heart of Dr. Pringle against Mr. Congdon and his friends.
In addition to that we have the resolution read by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) which embodies the views of the Young Men's Liberal Club of Dawson.
I have no doubt that every one here knows what that club was. The Liberals of the Yukon Territory, of Dawson City, lived for many years in harmony and then there occurred this cleavage. In the one hand were the Liberals whose head might be recognized as Mr. Congdon. On the other hand there were the Liberals of whom as pro-rninent a man as any was Dr. Pringle. They drifted apart until there was a cleavage and a new organization was formed early in the year 1904, about six months before the general elections. They formed a new organization absolutely different from the other and called themselves a Liberal club. They were men who were opposed to Mr. Congdon and his party, who would not recognize the convention that selected Mr. Congdon, but men who, one and all, supported Dr. Thompson, who always was and still is at heart an honest and consistent Conservative. They practically supported Dr. Thompson, the present member for the Yukon, in his election, and were most active, even taking the platform in that election opposing Mr. Congdon and supportihg Dr. Thompson. It is true that Dr. Thompson came here as an Independent, it is true that until that last night when he made his dramatic departure from here that he followed that course as an Independent. It is true also that he was always a Conservative, but out of consideration for his constituents he left the councils of the Conservative party. But, during the time he was in this House he never voted on want of confidence

motions, he consistently adhered to the position of an Independent and apart from the vote on the Autonomy Bill he always absented himself from votes, taking his course* manifestly and openly and saying that that was what he was doing. When he was about to catch the midnight train for Vancouver, expecting a dissolution of this House, he said that from that night on lie would be no longer an Independent. Thinking that he would not again appear in this parliament, he took occasion to say that he would return to his first love and his constant love, the Conservative party. It was that gentleman whom Dr. Pringle supported and at the same time he was very bold and very constant In his assertion that the only thing he had at heart was the good name of the Liberal party and the good name of Canada. I do not think we need read very much between the lines of his letters to conclude that Dr. Pringle was inspired by motives other than those which he wrote on the pages of those letters. We know the characters of the men who have been administrators of the Yukon. We know that they cannot for one moment be accused of a desire to shield immorality, graft, corruption or anything of that character. Let us start first with Commissioner Ogilvie. Then we have the Hon. James Hamilton Ross. These are two men whose honour I think nobody will question. They have neither loose views nor loose conduct with regard to morality or drunkenness or political corruption. Then take the next man, Mr. If. T. Congdon. Mr. Congdon may not be a brilliant success as a politician, he may not be an arch schemer, he may not be a good man to make devices and plans. I believe that in this respect Dr. Pringle can cut circles around him, but he is a man who no one will ever dare to say has loose views or conduct with regard to morality. I do not think that even the most careless speaker will ever say that he is loose in his views on even a moderate use of intoxicants or that he is a man with an inordinate desire to graft or be corrupt. I have never heard such a charge made against him and I am familiar with all of these charges. The charge that has been made Is that he had associates and employees under him in his position as Commisioner who have been open to suspicion, but I am confident I am stating the truth when I say that no responsible person will venture to assert that he is crooked or that he is a person who would in any way recognize, protect, encourage or tolerate corruption.
Then we have had the representatives of the Yukon in this House. The first was the Hon. James Hamilton Ross. I spoke of him a moment ago. Then we have the present member, Dr. Thompson. Those are the only two representatives we have had in this House from the Yukon. There again we have two men who represent Mr. KNOWLES.
public opinion a thousand times more than Dr. Pringle. They have sat here since 1900 but did they raise any voice of denunciation against this government ? Surely it was for them to say : The government is not endeavouring to enforce the laws in that land. It seems to me that it would have been their duty to do this had there been ground of complaint. Dr. Thompson's first duty was to represent the people of the Yukon, his one plank was that he would first and foremost represent the good opinion of the Yukon Territory in this House and apart from that he left party questions alone. Dr. Thompson is a man just as responsible as the reverend gentleman of whom I spoke, a man careful in his life, well advised in his views, a person who would not * be a party to corruption or immorality in any form. Messrs. Ross and Thompson have been here, they have come and gone and it has remained to this late date, when the public servants are crying out for their salaries, it remains for the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) after all these years to conclude that this question is so urgent and such a disgrace to the country that he cannot let the public servants have their salaries but he must discuss the affairs of the Yukon Territory. I take the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) at his word and I too will be pleased to see the effect this will have on the country. Here on the evening of the 2nd of June, when the cheques are already in arrears and the government desires to have money voted to pay the civil servants that they may not only not fall into debt but into the unprofitable habit of going into debt, the hon. member for North Toronto prevents the granting of supplies in order to discuss this question. It is a most serious thing and the country will appreciate its seriousness, that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) rises day after day to bring up such questions. The duty of bringing up this matter would have fallen on Senator Ross and Dr. Thompson and not particularly or properly on the hon. member for North Toronto.
But there is another conclusion I wish to draw from the silence of these gentlemen on the subject and it is that in view of this silence the presumption is altogether in favour of the accused. I do not for a moment say that it necessarily proves the innocence of these parties but I do take the stand that it makes a great presumption of innocence and that if this outrageous scandal had existed in the Yukon for all these years we would have heard of it from the representatives of the Yukon. If the charges of the hon. member for North Toronto are true it surely lays a most grave and serious reflection upon Dr. Thompson and Senator Ross, his predecessor.

May I say that the papers upon which the whole information has been

based were not brought down to this House until a few weeks ago ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Three months ago, the main return.
I do not think so, I had to ask for a supplementary return.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the 3rd of March, just three months ago.
Suppose it was three months ago.

Suppose they had not been brought down at all, would not Dr. Thompson and Senator Ross know enough to bring it to our attention if it had been such a public scandal as has been suggested? The truth is they did know the facts but knowing them they have not spoken about this matter. Surely, if there had been the open, public, outrageous scandal of which we have heard this afternoon, there would have been no trouble in Dr. Pringle finding many citizens well disposed towards decency and good government and desirous of maintaining decency in the conduct of public officials, to come and give their evidence before Commissioner Henderson. There are plenty of citizens in the Yukon who have just as strict and just as wholesome views with regard to public morality-and with regard to private morality too if you like-as Rev. Dr. Pringle has, or any of our friends opposite who have spoken on this subject, and who would be as strongly animated by a desire to keep clean the public life of their community. The Rev. Dr. Pringle is not so much holier or better than all the other citizens of the Yukon that, if there had been this glaring outrage, he would be the only man who would like to see a reform effected. The House will agree with me, I am sure, that, in such a case, there would have been plenty of people desirous of maintaining public morality who would come forward and give their testimony to support Dr. Pringle in bringing about a reform.
I am glad that the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) is now in his place as there is one remark which I wish respectfully to make with regard to what he said concerning the putting down of dance halls. He seemed to be determined that he would not admit that the Yukon government was primarily responsible in this matter or was really responsible at all. He seemed to say, in the first place, that Dr. Pringle was the initiator of the movement and afterwards seemed to say-and I am sure, did say-that it was really an act that this government was responsible for, in effect an act of this government and not of the Yukon Council. The hon. gentleman laid it down, I think, that everything done by the Yukon Council this government must get credit or blame for. I cannot understand the hon. gentleman taking that position. The Yukon Council surely exercises jurisdiction within the limits of the powers conferred upon it by the Yukon Act and amendments thereto, just as the provincial legislatures act within their jurisdiction by virtue of the British North America Act and the amendments thereto. The passing of such legislation, I submit, is wholly within the power of the Yukon Council; and I cannot for a moment understand my hon. friend making the statement that it is something for which this government must assume responsibility. And I was certainly very much surprised that the hon. gentleman should go so far as to say that Mr. Justice Dugas, who is Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the Yukon, in the discharge of his duties would be subject to political influence. I understood the hon. gentleman to say that; if I am wrong, I hope he will correct me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I wish to be governed by what I said, and not by the construction which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles) puts upon what I said. I may add, if the hon. gentleman will allow me, that what I stated in the first instance was that (Commissioner Henderson) procured the change in the law when he went there. That was disputed by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver).

With that statement I find no fault. I am corrected by the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) if he said that I am incorrect in believing that he implied or stated that Mr. Justice Dugas, in his opinion, would be influenced by political considerations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I used no such language.
I asked the hon. gentleman a question, and I understood him to say, ' Yes.'

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is mistaken; I made no direct allusion to Mr. Justice Dugas.

I asked the hon. gentleman directly and distinctly if he made that statement. I do not see how he can say he made no reference to Mr. Justice Dugas, for he answered my question. I made the reference in the first place, but the hon. gentleman answered.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is entirely in error. I gave no answer of that kind. I said that the government, by virtue of the fact that it appointed a majority of the members, could, at any time, control the council. The point on which issue was taken by the Minister of the Interior was that which I have mentioned just now. I said that Mr. Commissioner Henderson was responsible for having brought about the change, and I said

that he had done it because Dr. Pringle had brought the subject to his attention. I afterwards read Commissioner Henderson's own report in which he declared that, having had his attention directed to the subject by Dr. Pringle's letter, he had canvassed every member of the council and procured the necessary change in the legislation to be introduced by Mr. .Justice Dugas. and it was passed upon his initiative.
Well, of course, I accept the hon. gentleman's statement, which, I have no doubt, is correct. I understood him differently, and I believe that other hon. members on this side understood him as I did.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They misunderstood me.
I am sure of it. However, the hon. gentleman did say that the Yukon Council was subject to the control of this government

L, BORDEN. Certainly.
Mr. KNOWLES

in its legislation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Certainly.
And X understood that control was not only in the way of the veto, but control in the ordinary sense.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In other words, it is in the power of this government to enforce its policy in the Yukon by reason of the control it has over the membership of that council.
That would be possible only by way of removal of members of the council and the appointment of people who are nothing but tools in the hands of the government, and
You would not call them tools if they carried out the policy of the government?

Certainly, if they were not true to their own opinions and to their oaths, I would call them tools. That is what I said, and that is what I shall be ready to say to-morrow. I was about to say that I understood the leader of the opposition to say that the law which was passed with regard to gambling houses and dance halls was a law which was made by reason of the fact that it was desired by this government. If so, I am confident that he does not do justice to the gentlemen who are members of the council, especially to the learned judge who is a member of that council, in thinking that that learned gentleman would fail to use his own good judgment and be true to his oath of office. I am sure the leader of the opposition could not, on reflection, renew that statement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Apparently, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles! has not un-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
derstood me yet. What I intended to suggest, and what I desire to adhere to is that if the government of this country found the men appointed to the Yukon Council persisted in maintaining a policy and a system under which the most notorious houses of prostitution in the shape of dance halls were run in that country, it would be possible for this government, if it found remonstrances with these gentlemen unavailing, to dismiss them from their office and appoint men who would not allow that condition to continue.
The hon. gentleman will correct me if I am wrong. He will agree that that could have no influence upon the present action of the council in Dawson?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am speaking of the supposed control of the government of the Yukon Council.

I think the hon. gentleman cannot understand the point to which I am referring-his contention, as I understand it, that the legislation under which the dance halls were driven out was the result of the desire of the government at Ottawa and not the result of the judgment of the Council of the Yukon.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On the contrary, I stated that it was the result of Mr. Commissioner Henderson's initiative-that he went to the Yukon and, having had his attention called to the matter by the Rev. Dr. Pringle, took steps which resulted in this change.

Very well, let it go. The charge is so flat that I felt disposed not to speak at all. I was willing, however, to say a few words; but really, the attack is dead, and it seems almost like abusing the dead to go on with this discussion.
Even the father of it has run away.

It is further to be observed, as you will see by reference to the file, that Dr. Pringle has stated that he has charges only against two men. Mr. Pringle informed the commission to this effect, as you will see in the commissioner's letter, addressed to Hon. Frank Oliver, dated September 23, 1907.
He says:
He informed me that he had no charges to make against any person in the employ of the government other than Messrs. Girouard and Litligow.
In regard to these two gentlemen, and these are all that a royal commission could deal with, one of them is out of the service of the government and I do not see anything so very urgent about his case that the public supply should be stopped to deal with it. With regard to Mr. Litligow, he

is a gentleman who was brought into the public service by lion, gentlemen opposite, he has been kept in the public service by this government because he is a good official and I do not think that any one in the Yukon or out of it will say that he has ever been guilty of neglect of duty or malfeasance in office. He is a very superior man, a good official and the public service has not suffered by the fact that this gentleman has been kept in the employ of the government. The fact that he has been kept in the public service is no reason why the supplies should be held up and the public servants should lose their monthly pay. Mr. Lithgow, Mr. Girouard and Mr. Pringle sat for years together in the Yukon council, and Mr. Pringle never raised any objection when they stood as equals upon the floor of the local legislature. It is very strange that it took him all these years to find these things out about Mr. Lithgow and Mr. Girouard.
The bon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) spoke with regard to the Governor General's letter. He seemed to say that the Governor General's letter was instrumental in bringing the government to a condition of action. It is very clear that the Minister of the Interior received a communication from the secretary of the Governor General and from Mr. Pringle at the same time, that is the first communication he ever had from Mr. Pringle, so that it is impossible that he or the government should only have been stirred to action by the receipt of a communication from the secretary of the Governor General. It is not fair or worthy of the hon. leader of the opposition to advance the argument that it was the letter of the private secretary of the Governor General that stirred the minister up. If that were so it would be very easy to get anything done because any man, upon writing to the government, could also drop a note to the Governor General and the Governor General's secretary could say that such and such a letter had been received. I want to read the opening part of the letter of the 28th August, written by the Minister of the Interior to the Rev John Pringle:
Your letter of July 31, was brought to my attention on my return from an extended trip to the west, which began on July 19th and ended on Monday, August 26.
Only two days before this letter was written.
I was, therefore, not in Ottawa when your letter arrived, and was consequently unable to reply to it before. Since my return I have received a letter from the Governor General's secretary informing me that His Excellency had received a copy of the same letter. The premier had also informed me (that on receipt of the copy of the letter sent to him he communicated with Messrs. Girouard and Lithgow the allegations made <by yourself against them.
Showing that the point that was made by the hon. leader of the opposition, that the Minister of the Interior was moved to action by the fact that Mr. Pringle saw fit to write to the Governor General was not quite fair.
There has been a good deal said this afternoon about the lax way in which justice is administered in the Yukon and these statements have been made upon a very feeble foundation, such as the letter which the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) read, signed by ' Bona fide.'
That is a good name.
It is a good name, and it is a name that any rascal can make use of.
That is rather an imputation on ' Bona fide.' You should not do that.

them prevail, and citizens have the same right to complain and complaints, so far as I know, are listened to.
There has been no specific charge in the papers. I don't know what the complaint is. But I say that, speaking broadly and generally, it is unfair to the Yukon territory-I do not care about myself-and unfair to the officials that statements should go abroad that law generally is not generally enforced in the rukon territory. I know of no mining camp where law is so well observed, where men and women are so safe in going about the streets as they are in this camp.
I regret to have to make these remarks, but I feel it to be my duty-not personally, mind you, but as an official charged with the prosecution of the law in this country-to say that I know of no case where the law has not been enforced, and I know of no case where the law has been asked to be enforced and refusal made.

Might I remind the hon. gentleman that I brought to the notice of this House, some few years ago, a specific case where two men were fined, and, I think, imprisoned for taking timber without a permit when the timber dues had been paid and when they desired to appeal and when they attempted to get the evidence which they had a right to get it was denied them over and over again, they could not get it and they have not got it to this day.

I think I am familiar with the case that the hon. gentleman refers to, but if I understand that case, it was simply that the machinery of the criminal law was called in when it should never have been called in; it was such a trivial matter. I understand that the charge of hon. gentlemen opposite is that In important matters the criminal law is not called in. The hon. gentleman has gone back year after year; I do not know how many years he has gone back to bring these cases up. He told us this afternoon about a whisky contract twelve years old. That is getting pretty old and probably if whisky is that old it will be better than when they took it in. Our hon. friends opposite are fond of bringing up these matters of great age, and so we hear session after session of the * Arctic,' the North Atlantic Trading Company, the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company, the Yukon liquor permits, always the same old accusations. We have wasted this whole day upon a matter that is many years old, that has been before the public as an outstanding scandal during all these years, and it is only at this late date that they again repeat the story for the purpose of delaying the business of the House.

Considering the eagerness of my hon. friend from West Assiniboia (Mr. Knowles) not to waste the time of the House he has delivered rather a long and Mr. KNOWLES.
pointless defence of what he calls a dead attack made by the opposition. Had he the courage of his convictions he would have said nothing, or else he would have said something to the point. The matter is in a nutshell. The first question is : Who makes this attack, and the answer is : The Rev. John Pringle. And Mr. Pringle is, as he says in his letter of the 27th of May, 1902 :
I am the Presbyterian minister at Bonanza. I am a citizen of Canada by birth, a Liberal by conviction, believing that the triumph of Liberal princples is the triumph of might.
Is Dr. Pringle alone in his attack? Not at all. On the 13th November, 1907, at the regular meeting of the Young Men's Liberal Club, composed of what may be called the decent young Liberals of' the Yukon Territory, a resolution was passed which unanimously confirmed the statements of the Rev. Dr. Pringle. Now, I have the honour of knowing the Rev. Dr. Pringle I have been in the Yukon and I can say that I did not find there a man who waa more highly respected and more generally revered by the people of the Territory than was the Rev. Dr. Pringle. When you find such a man simply committing the sin of being a Liberal of the old school attached to true Liberal principles, and when you find him supported by the decent young Liberals of the country, one would think that a good tactician and able statesman like the Prime Minister would be able to-discern that the Rev. Dr. Pringle was telling the truth and not the man who wanted to retain office at all hazard. What interest had the Rev. John Pringle, a Liberal by birth, a man highly respected, one of the leading divines of the Presbyterian Church, what interest had he to tell lies? There can be no suggestion that he had the slightest possible Interest In doing so. But the other men who contradicted him, the men who wish to retain office, the men whose living depended on their retaining office, they had an interest in refuting the statements of Dr. Pringle, and it is the statement of such men that the Prime Minister takes as against the statement of Dr. Pringle, supported as it is by the young Liberals of the Yukon. The right hon. gentleman says that in 1902 there was no charges of a specific character. It is a peculiarity of the Prime Minister and those associated with him that they never are able to find a specific charge when they don't want to investigate. But if the right hon. gentleman will peruse the letter of the 27th November, 1902, he will find there a charge sufficiently specific to warrant investigation. This document came to the Prime Minister from a Liberal by conviction, and it came from a reverend gentleman entitled to the highest respect, although it has suited hon. gentlemen opposite to-day to cast aspersions on the Rev.
