Dr. Pringle. In 1902 Dr. Pringle brought to the attention of the Prime Minister the subject of hydraulic concessions, then a question of live interest in the Yukon, and because of which considerable ill-feeling was engendered against the government of the day, it being stated, and I believe truely, that a great many valuable concessions that could have been worked successfully by the miners themselves had been given to certain favourites of the Liberal party. It is true that the present Minister of the Interior has properly seen fit to cancel certain of these concessions, but the fact remains that as far back as 1902 this question was brought to the attention of the First Minister and this business administration went asleep until 1906 over a matter of such vital importance to the people of the Yukon Territory. The reverend gentleman goes on to say :
Concessions have been granted, I am convinced, not only carelessly, buit indquitously; the heritage of out people given to satisfy the greed of capital, without due consideration of the rights of the people in the ground, or of the character of the statements made to secure these concessions.
The government said this was not specific enough, and so they did not take the trouble to investigate it and to see whether the statement was true. The reverend gentleman complained of the dance halls in which some of the government officials were frequenters, and he says:
But the worst feature of the licensed houses here is that a very large percentage of them are houses of prostitution. Many of them run, it is true, by people of good character. But a large number of bawdy houses, with a government license to prey upon the public.
He says further :
The law is systematically manipulated, not to protect the public but to proteat and nurse the gambler and shame honest men.
The government saw fit to take no action with regard to these charges. On the 3rd of January, 1905, another letter came to the First Minister, and the specific charges in that letter were such as to demand investigation at the hands of any well meaning government. Mr. Pringle's fairness is shown by the fact that he is glad to concede the part that Mr. Ross, as Yukon Commissioner, took in putting down the abuses referred to, and be points out that these abuses have again arisen and are in fuller swing than they were before Mr. Ross took means to mitigate the evil. But instead of investigating the matter the Prime Minister simply takes the word of the men charged against the statements of the Rev. Dr. Pringle, who could have no personal interest in the matter. And so it was allowed to rest until 1907, when charges were again made, and the Minister of the Interior on the 28th of August, 1907, wrote to the Hon. Alexander Henderson a letter which, although it has been already read, it is proper to read again, because in my judgment it is the key to the whole situation. The letter says :
Dear Sir,-I beg to inclose herewith copy of a letter received by me from the Governor General's office. As you will note from the address and contents, the original of this letter was adressed to the premier and to myself.	.
You will be good enough to investigate fully the specific charges made by Mr. Pringle against Messrs. Girouard and Lithgow, and will, of course, call upon Mr. Pringle to substantiate those charges. You are to investigate fully and report.
Should the Rev. Mr. Pringle desire to lay charges against any other persons in the employ of the government, or of the Interior Department especially, you are to investigate them as well.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) FRANK OLIVER.
The point of that letter is simply this. If the Minister of the Interior is to be taken at his word, if he is to be bound by that letter, be is of opinion that there were charges to be investigated, and if so, there was, as he knows only one proper method of investigating a charge of a public character. If those charges were charges against those gentlemen in their private capacity-and I am passing no opinion on the truth or falsity of the charges themselves-it was not the business of the Minister of the Interior to investigate them. He had a right to investigate the charges only if they came under part 1 or part 2 of chapter 104 of the Act respecting Public and Departmental inquiries. I agree with the First Minister that they do not come under part 2, and that if they come under any part of that Act they come under part 1, which provides :
Th Govenor in Council may, whenever he deems at expedient, cause inquiry to be made into and concerning any matter conneoted with the good government of Canada or the conduct o-f any part of the public business thereof.
Under that section the government could have investigated the concessions referred to, the abuse of the license system, the character of any of the officials of the government so far as it affected the good government of Canada. If there was any right to investigate at all, there was only one proper form of investigation, for an obvious reason. Does any sensible man in this House think, with the character of the material on which these charges are based, that any one would voluntarily come forward and give testimony before the commissioner ? They would not do so, for two reasons : they would have no protection at the hands of the court, and they would lay themselves open, whether they were

telling the truth or not, to a charge of slander ; and that Is what has happened, for an action for libel has been brought against the Rev. John Pringle. Furthermore, you could not compel witnesses to come forward and give evidence. It is years ago that some of the events charged took place. Witnesses to these events might not be in the Yukon at the time of the investigation ; their conduct money would have to be paid, wherever they might be, and they would certainly have to be subpoenaed and if they gave their evidence under compulsion, it would have to be before a tribunal that could give them ample protection. If the Minister of the Interior really desired an investigation, he was in duty bound to have a proper investigation under the Act, as Mr. Pringle demanded. Well, what happened ? Mr. Henderson, on the 8th of November, 1907, wrote to Mr. Oliver as follows :
Dear Mr. Oliver,

I am inclosing herewith a copy of the correspondence relating to the charges of the Rev. Dr. Pringle against Messrs. Grirouard and Litbgow. You will see from Dr. Pringle's letter to * of the 23rd ultimo, he declines to appear as a party in what he calls an informal investigation. I would suggest, if agreeable to you, that I be appointed a commissioner to investigate the charges under the provisions of the Inquiries Act, chapter 101, Revised Statutes of Canada. 1906.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) ALEXANDER HENDERSON, Commissioner.
In that connection, I want to call attention to a further letter written by Mr. Henderson to the Rev. John Pringle, as follows :
Dawson, Yukon Territory, October 30, 1907.
Sir,-Pn reply to your communication of the 23rd instant, in which you inform me that you must adhere to your decision contained in your letter of the 11th instant, not to take any part in the informal investigation into the charges against Messrs. Laihgow and Girouard, I beg to say that I am requesting from the government that authority be given to me to investigate the charges on the lines of a commission, which will enable me to issue summonses and to take the evidence of witnesses under oath. I trust this course will be deemed satisfactory.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) ALEXANDER HENDERSON, Commission, Yukon Territory.
That was -a letter from the commissioner of the Yukon and a lawyer to the Rev. Mr. Pringle, conceding his position that an informal investigation could not be satisfai? tory, but that the proper course was that Mr. Henderson should be appointed a commissioner under the Act. He writes to the minister suggesting such an Investigation, and the minister says, no, I will not have Mr. BRISTOL.
it. And so, as the Minister of the Interior and the government did not desire any real investigation, but wanted to bury these charges in oblivion, the minister goes back on bis original promise to have an investigation, and they do nothing at all but endeavour to cover up and conceal one of the worst scandals that disgraces the administration of this government.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) desired to avail himself of this matter as a convenient opportunity to occupy another day and thus prevent the progress of the very urgent and proper business of the House, the passage of the supplies which are necessary for the carrying on of the King's government, I must admit at once that he has quite achieved his purpose. But if he had any other object in view, I confess that I am utterly unable to discover it. Why the hon, gentleman should bring this matter up at all at this moment, if he had any other purpose in view, is difficult to understand. The matter is not new. This story of V uIcon difficulties has been before the country a considerable time. My hon. friend has suggested that the Rev. Mr. Pringle is the first man who has had the courage to refer to these dreadful things that occurred in the Yukon. That was hardly just to a very distinguished mem-l)6r of this parliament who a few years ago made a speech of seven hours in "making accusations of a general character with reference to Yukon affairs, and, finding that he had omitted one or two things, made another speech of eight or nine hours to make up the deficiency. Perhaps the fact that that gentleman, though a very able man. failed to accomplish very much by his attack, may have been the reason that from time to time we heard less and less about these Yukon scandals.
Nor do we forget that, in connection with a discussion of that kind, the distinguished leader of the opposition of that day, making charges of a general character, such as those made to-day-in which my hon. friend wandered over the whole history of tile ^ ukon-went so far as to mention the name of one of the citizens of Canada and accused him of graft. But when that citizen took action in the courts of the country to vindicate himself and bring his accuser to account, Sir Charles Tupper, promptly climbed down and made a humble apology to the person aggrieved. And I am inclined to think that if we were to pass from generalities and come down to particulars, the same experience would follow to-day as did then. In this matter one or two gentlemen, whose names are freely mentioned, are personally known to me. I refer particularly to Messrs. Congdon and Lithgow.

There is really little against Mr. Congdon although his name figures in Mr. Pringle's correspondence pretty extensively. When we come down however to specific statements, we do not find any accusation against him. What we find are statements of a personal character against Messrs. Lithgow and Girouard. If I heard the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) rightly a moment ago, he considered that there was nothing to investigate. I understood him to say that the Minister of the Interior could only have the right to investigate matters affecting the official conduct of persons in his employ, and that it would be no part of his duty to have an investigation into their private character. Unless, therefore, there is a charge made against them in their official capacity, the Minister of the Interior had no right to order an investigation at all. Mr. BRISTOL. I was not expressing an opinion on the charges but was simply commenting on the fact that the minister had ordered an investigation, and I was pointing out that the investigation would not be into charges merely of a personal character but into charges with respect to conduct in the performance of a public duty. Mr. FIELDING. That is quite right. If the charges were of a personal character and had no relation to public duties, the Minister of the Interior had no right to order an investigation at all. Mr. BRISTOL. But he did order one. Mr. FIELDING. I am giving the view which the hon. member for Centre Toronto expressed. The public records show that although there were general charges and statements covering the whole administration of the Yukon, when we read the correspondence and sift the whole matter down, it resolves itself into mere personal charges against the private character of these gentlemen and nothing more. And according to my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol), those are not proper subjects for an official inquiry. I have here the letter of the 2nd October, 1907, written by Mr. Pringle to Mr. Henderson, in which he specifies his charges against Mr. Lithgow and Mr. Girouard. Mr. Pringle says : I am prepared for the investigation which you have been instructed to hold into the charges which I have made of scandalous living on the part of J. T. Lithgow and J. E. Girouard, prominent public servants in the Yukon. I am prepared to prove	 And then he goes on to state his charges in clauses 1, 2 and 3. These clauses I do not wish to quote because I am not anxious to needlessly advertise the very improper charges made. But every one of these paragraphs has reference to the	personal and private life of the two gentlemen named. Mr. BRISTOL. But if the personal character of au official of the government was such as to create the conviction that he was unfit for the position, would not that be a matter for investigation ? Mr. FIELDING. I am not discussing the purely legal question as to whether these accusations would come under the term of any particular Act. But what right would the Minister of the Interior have to appoint a royal commission to investigate unless the matter to be investigated were one affecting official conduct ? Mr. tBRISTOL. But he did. Mr. FIELDING. I do not think he would have any right to appoint a royal commission and in my opinion the demand for such a commission was most absurd. Mr. BRISTOL. The commissioner of the Yukon and an ex-judge thought it very proper. Mr. FIELDING. I have known eminent judges to differ in these matters. I would not set my own opinion as a layman against that of a judge, but judges like doctors often differ. I take my hon. friend's opinion that the Minister of the Interior had no right, as a matter of common sense and reason, to investigate a mere charge against the private character of any man. Suppose that in Montreal or Ottawa some good citiezn-even a Christian (minister of the high rank of Mr. Pringle-should write a letter to the Minister of Customs in which he expressed his belief that a certain collector of customs or other customs official in some district was leading an immoral life, would it be reasonable to demand that a royal commission should be appointed to investigate into such a charge? It may be a question whether the minister would be justified in taking any notice of such a letter. If he thought the matter sufficiently serious, he might send some official down to call on the man accused and give him an opportunity to explain and then make a report, but no one would seriously contend that it was a proper matter for an investigation by a Royal Commission. Suppose some Toronto officer-especially a good Conservative appointed many years ago-were accused of improper conduct in his private capacity, and the government were to appoint a roval commission, on the strength of such ail accusation, to investigate into this man's private life, my hon. friend from Centre Toronto would be the first to complain that the investigation was a case of political persecution. Putting aside for a moment this idea that there is something extraordinary about this Yukon affair, and treating it as we would any other case that

might arise any time in the public service, it will be at once seen how unreasonable was the demand for a royal commission. The curious part of it all is that what Mr. Pringle tells us was so notorious does not appear to have been notorious in the mind of anybody else. He says that the conduct of these men was for years a matter of public notoriety. Well, the commissioners of the Yukon have been men of undoubted high character, honesty and repute, and they have not reported anv such terrible condition of affairs. The Minister of the Interior himself went out to the Yukon to ascertain the facts and find out for himself what were the conditions existing there. Surely if this matter were of the great notoriety described by Mr. Pringle, when the minister arrived at the government office or his hotel in Dawson city, he would have been met by men in that city who would have told him the true condition of things. But while he receievd complaints concerning a good many other matters, not one word did he hear against the reputation or the conduct off these men, whose conduct Mr Pringle says was a matter of public notoriety and great scandal to the community. Do not imagine for a moment that I am questioning the zeal or the good motives of Mr. Pringle. But we know that often well meaning men, animated by the best intentions, allow their zeal to outrun their discretion. Any one who reads Mr. Pringle's letters will find that, whether he was influenced by personal motives or not, he has made remarkable statements and used very strong language. For instance, in one of his letters he takes the trouble to repeat the story that one of the Christian ministers of the city of Dawson accepted contributions from the dance halls and other places of ill repute upon the condition that he would keep his mouth closed.
I would like my hon. friend to give the quotation. I have read that letter carefully and I do not think it bears that interpretation.

I would like to ask what the ministers of the gospel in Dawson and throughout the Yukon will think of the wisdom of Dr. Pringle in sending that accusation against them, for it is against them, in a letter to the Prime Minister of Canada.
Dr. Pringle in that letter had a good deal to say about concessions and mentioned particularly what is "known as the Bronson and Ray concession. He said that in the Bronson and Ray concession none of the conditions upon which it was granted have been fulfilled. He said it was easy to cancel it. speechtext:
I do not know. For my present purpose it is not very important. I simply want to mention it as another illustration that my friend Dr. Pringle is zealous in making rash statements about matters as to which he has no better information than the rest of mankind.
I repeat that the interest I feel in the matter is largely a personal interest as respects the gentlemen concerned. I have already said that there is no accusation against Mr. Congdon, although his name is frequently mentioned. He was a very eminent barrister among the younger bar of the province of Nova Scotia, a man of undoubted ability and the highest character, and whatever may be said about his conduct in political matters in the Yukon, I must say that no man who ever knew him in Nova Scotia would have the slightest doubt that in everything that makes for a clean life and for a high moral standard and integrity of character he sustained his reputation in the west.
With regard to Mr. Lithgow I feel an interest because I had something to do with his appointment. In the early days of the Yukon, the ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) came to me to discuss financial arrangements for the Yukon and we agreed that it was necessary to have a very capable and strong man in there to deal with that branch of the public business. Mr. Sifton suggested that I should recommend a man who would be satisfactory to the Finance department. I took time to consider it and selected Mr. Lithgow. In view of the suggestions that there is some political end to serve,' that there was some favour to be done for our political friends, it is worth mentioning, although it is not important, that Mr. Lithgow was no political friend of mine. I have known him from boyhood and he has always been a Conservative. His father, a very eminent citizen of Halifax, who has recently passed away, was not only a Conservative, known to be warmly in sympathy with the Conservative party, but in one of the political campaigns of which I have a very lively recollection, he was one of the leading writers in the public press in the support of the Conservative party. The Lithgows, father and son, and every member of the family, so far as I have ever known, have belonged to the Conservative party. John T. Lithgow came into the service of the government when the Conservatives were in power. He was appointed to the Halifax branch of the Finance Department by Sir Leonard Tilley. He has been twenty-eight years in the public service. He had served there under several ministers and when I came into office I knew enough of him to value his character, capacity and service. When I had an opportunity of either promoting a man, for it was a promotion, or * bringing a man from the outside, I selected

him, notwithstanding his known Conservative proclivities and recommended him to the Minister of the Interior, and he was sent to the Yukon. So I felt an interest in the matter. I am bound to say that notwithstanding all that has happened, I have never found a shadow of reason for regretting that I recommended the Minister of the Interior to appoint Jack Lithgow, as everyone knew him in Halifax. He is a man well known throughout the maritime provinces and I believe wherever he was known he was respected, irrespective of all consideration of politics or anything else. He went out to that country at a time when there were very great difficulties. He passed through that period when officials on all sides were being accused of wrongdoing- most frequently I hope without just cause -and Mr. Lithgow passed unscathed through all the stormy times of the Yukon administration. I never met a man, until this letter of Dr. Pringle's was presented, who knew anything about the Yukon who did not bear testimony to the value and faithful services of John T. Lithgow. I want to say that for him now. I believe that Mr. Lithgow has had his faults; I believe that, so far as I have been able to make inquiries, on one occasion he permitted himself to stray from the path of sobriety. I believe that on one occasion he did himself discredit. But it is but fair to say that there are but few men who can submit to have applied to them the severe standard that never on any occasion shall they have allowed themselves to depart from the line of propriety. Notwithstanding the fact that, on that occasion, the man was at fault, I say he has been a most faithful, useful and valuable servant of Canada, and it would be a scandal and a shame if he were dismissed for that one fault. And I want to emphasize the fact that this is purely a matter affecting Mr. Lithgow's personal character. Even Dr. Pringle does not allege that Mr. Lithgow has failed in his duty. True, he did, in one passage, make a reference to Mr. Lithgow, which, I am sure, he could not sustain and which, I am equally sure, will not be accepted by any friend who has known Mr. Lithgow. He spoke not only of Mr. Lithgow's personal character, but in a passage which I thought I had at hand, he stated that Mr. Lithgow had been working in the interest of the gang of thieves who had been having both hands in the public treasury. Mr. Pringle is the only man I have ever heard who would make any such accusation against Mr. Lithgow. The universal testimony of friend and foe is that, through all these troublous times, this man proved himself exceptionally qualified for his duties and performed his duties with great ability and fidelity.
Reference is made in the papers to a resolution said to have been passed by the Mr FIELDING
Young Men's Liberal Club of Dawson, opposing a movement said to be on foot for the appointment of Mr. Lithgow as commissioner. If that Young Men's Liberal Club did pass such a resolution, it was pretty good evidence of the fact that the government were not dealing with the matter in a partisan way, for, whatever favour and consideration they gave to Mr. Lithgow, they did not give through the influence of the young Liberals of that territory. Lithgow, controller, as being unfit to occupy the position that he now holds. I beg to state that I am not in accord with said resolution and have refused to sign it.

So, the meeting to which reference has been made appears to have been a very small meeting, and the very chairman who presided over this deliberations took the trouble to write this letter to the Prime Minister explaining that he did not approve of the resolution and had refused to sign it.
Now, I want to press an argument referred to by others and to which In a word by the way this afternoon, I alluded. Hon. gentlemen have quoted from Dr. Pringle the statement that the election of Dr. Thompson iu the Yukon was brought about as a vindication of the rights of the decent people of the Yukon and as a protest against dance halls, gambling hells and that sort of thing. If we accept that as true, then Dr. Thompson, when he came to this House was to be recognized as the interpreter of that sentiment. That bon. gentleman sat here year after year; he was personally familiar with this matter and was chosen especially to represent it; and yet not on one occasion did he venture to rise In his place and make any such accusations concerning any official as have been made in his absence by the hon. member for North Toronto. I think the public mind will regard that fact as important. It is only reasonable to suppose that, if the public conscience in Dawson had been so shocked, if these matters were of such public notoriety, if a great wrong had been done and the public service had scandalized the community, and if no remedy had been afforded for these things, surely the man elected by the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite, elected and sent to the House to remedy such abuses, would have stood up in this House, explained and denounced'the

abuses and demanded a remedy. Yet that hon. gentleman sat in his place here year after year, even long after these papers had been brought before the House, and never raised his voice in condemnation. I venture to draw the conclusion that that hon. gentleman, who knew Mr. Lithgow and knew the facts, was satisfied that the public interest was best served, and would continue to be best served, by keeping Mr. John T. Lithgow in the office which he has filled so ably and so successfully.
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Cavil government-Department of the Interior, $190,012.50.
Will the Minister of the Interior give us a statement of the increases and changes that have been made in the officers of this department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The vote asked for civil government, salaries, is $190,012.50. The vote last year was $182,050, there being an increase of $7,962.50. This is made up bv statutory increases, $4,925 ; promotions, $5,000 ; difference in estimating for the salaries of three third-class clerks, $137.50 ; then there is deducted $2,100, decrease in salaries occasioned by promotions and changes, and the $7,962.50 is accounted for.
The minister has fourteen chief clerks whereas last year he had twelve. Have two been promoted to chief clerkships?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. J. M. Roberts and Mr. P. Marchand have been promoted from the position of first-class clerks to be chief clerks. Mr. Roberts is in charge of the registration branch and Mr. Marchand is deputy or assistant to the chief accountant.
Have these chief clerkships been created yet?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, these offices have been created by order in council and we are now asking for monej to meet the salaries.
What is Mr. Roberts' sal-arv at present?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: $1,500, and we desire to make it $1,900.
How long has Mr. Roberts been in that branch?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Since 1900.

In what position and at what salary?
Air. OLIA7ER. He came in as a temporary clerk at $900. He was employed at first in the timber and mines branch, afterwards removed to the registration branch and finally promoted to the chiefship of the registration branch.
When was he made a permanent clerk?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: At what salary?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: That would be a second-class clerji?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A senior second.
When was he promoted after that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He was made a first-class clerk in 1906 at $1,500. I was in error in saying that his present salary is $1,500; it is $1,550.
What does he get as chief clerk?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Does the minister not think that has been pretty rapid progress?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it is rapid.
What have been the influences which have been at work to make this rapid progress?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The influence is the ability of Air. Roberts. I am not aware of any other influence.
Where did Air. Roberts come from?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not answer that.

The minister will see that this is a very rapid stride forward. Here is a young man who, seven years ago, was not in the service at all ; he comes in as a temporary clerk in 1900 and gets $900; in 1903 he is made permanent as a second-class clerk at $1,100, not at the minimum of the second class ; in 1900 he is up to $1,500, and now, in 1908, he is to go in as a chief clerk at a minimum of $1,900. He increases from $900 to $1,900. There must be some very pressing reason why Air. Roberts has such rapid promotion as that over a great many clerks who have been in that department for a much longer period and who must have a great deal more experience without doubt. As to whether they have more ability will be for the minister to say.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are not removing Mr. Roberts to any other position but we want to make him of higher rank in proportion to his work and responsibility.
His work will be just the same and this is a way the minister has of adding $400 to his salary and giving him a chance to get $500 or $600 more.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the idea.

The minister is bound to tell the House what are the superior abil-

ities of Mr. Roberts which entitle him to this galloping speed upwards. There is no superhuman ability required to do that work. Can the minister say that the clerks in the department who have experience added to their abilities are not able to do that work and that Mr. Roberts must be jumped up ? His rapid promotion must be for some other reason that the minister has given.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know of no other reason. Any one who is familiar with the operation of such a department knows that upon careful and reliable registration depends the proper transaction of the business. While the registration seems to be a matter of mere detail, in practice it has not been found so. Mr. J. J. Henry had been in charge of the branch for twenty years when his health failed, not because of his age but because of the onerous character of the work which broke him down, and it became necessary to give him some other employment. There are some forty clerks in the branch and there has to be most careful management and the work of the department depends on the work of these men being properly done. After Mr. Henry ' we tried one or two of the staff and found they were not able to cope with the work and at last we selected Mr. Roberts. Since his appointment we find the work is well and promptly done, that there is order and promptitude where formerly such was not the case. Mr. Roberts is in the full vigour of life and he seems to have special aptitude for organization and management. We recognize that it is due in a very considerable degree to the proper management of this branch that we have been able to carry on so well as we have the stupendously increased business of the department. It has already been brought to the attention of the House that men of higher abilities and higher responsibilities are not as a rule paid wages equal to what they could earn outside and we have lost several men from the department because of that. It is a fair business proposition that when we have a man who is able to take a responsible position and is in the full vigour of life we should pay him according to the work he does. It is on that principle I have asked parliament to increase Mr. Roberts' salary.
Did Mr. Roberts become a civil servant through the regular door or was he made a civil servant by Act of parliament ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Roberts came In as a temporary at first; he afterwards passed his civil service examination and entered the permanent service in the usual way.
But not at the minimum of the second class.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He was made permanent at the minimum of the second class.
In what year did he pass the civil service examination ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not able to answer that.	.

You say you want to keep this official and give him a good salary but you must recollect there are at least thirty men in the department who are ahead of him and you may be doing a great injustice to some of these. Will the minister say that not one of these thirty men has the method and habits which would enable him to do the work of the registration branch ? Has there been any examination to test the ability of the others ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When Mr. Henry unfortunately had to give up his position. I think attempts were made to fill it with one or two other gentlemen, but they were not able to meet the requirements. We did not go through the whole list, because when Mr. Roberts got the opportunity he filled the bill, and I admit that it was of more interest to us to get the work well done than to go through the whole list of employees to find out if more than one of them could do the work.

Yes, but the opportunity was given to the newcomer and the old hands were not given the opportunity. Then, what reason has the minister for making Mr. Roberts, who has been only a short time in the service, a chief clerk, where he is doing no more efficiently the same work that he has been doing since 190G, and adding $400 to his salary? Could he not have done the business just as well on the lower salary? Have his few years of service in the department earned him that promotion and that high salary, while others have been twenty years in the department, and have been doing faithful and honest and efficient work during that time, and do not yet receive as much? Is it not a fact that Mr. Roberts has been the nominee of the chief whip of the Liberal party, and that he owes his rapid promotion to that influence?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot say what connection there may be between Mr. Roberts and the chief whip of the Liberal party; but I can say certainly that I have no knowledge of any such connection-that the chief whip never spoke to me about Mr. Roberts, and certainly Mr. Roberts never spoke to me about the chief whip. In fact, he has never spoken to me about his position. What has been done has been done upon the representations of the

deputy in the ordinary way and upon my own knowledge of Mr. Roberts' efficiency in the transaction of business. I might say that Mr. Henry, the previous occupant of the position, was receiving $2,300 a year, and I do not think it is unreasonable that Mr. Roberts, who is doing the same work *-in fact, a great deal more work, because the business has increased very much- should be put in the position to ultimately get the same salary as Mr. Henry got. I do not wish to disparage Mr. Henry's work, but I am bound to say that the work is being better done now than it was under Mr. Henry.
What has been Mr. Mar-chand's course?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Marchand entered the service in 1899 as a second-class clerk at $1,100 a j'ear.
Did he pass the civil service examination?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He informs me that he passed the civil service examination in 1S99.
And when did his first promotion take place?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He was made a first-class clerk in 1901 at $1,500.
And he is now receiving $1,650?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

These are two examples of extremely rapid promotions, one of the men having been brought into the service in 1899 and the other in 1900, and in the short space of seven or eight years they have risen to be chief clerks. I am not in a position to rate the merits of either of these men, but it seems to me somewhat peculiar and somewhat unfair that employees of that department who entered the service at the minimum rate find after a service of twenty or twenty-five years that men are brought in and put right over them, commencing at high salaries, and being now chief clerks. It does not seem to me to be right or fair. Surely the minister is not going to make the confession that amongst all the horde of clerks that he has in the Interior Department, good and capable servants I believe, he could not find any two fit to be made chief clerks. There does not seem to be much incentive to a spirit of work and enterprise amongst the body of the civil servants if the prizes are to be bestowed in this way.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot answer for the reasons for the previous promotions of these two gentlemen; but for the present promotion, for which, of course, I am responsible, directly and indirectly, I may say that it is simply due to the recognition of efficiency. and a desire to retain that effi 308
ciency in the service by paying such wages as are in accordance with the service rendered. It is to be regretted that all cannot be at the top, and I am not prepared to say that there may not be other men in the department just as competent as the two mentioned.
I think the minister ought to be able to say that before he makes the rapid promotion of these two men.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the House will realize that in dealing with a department having 585 employees in the city of Ottawa, if the minister or his chief officers were to occupy the time that would be necessary to see that no injustice was done by promotions amongst all that staff of officials, they would hardly be giving that attention to the public business for which they are paid and which the country expects from them. It is an unfortunate situation, but I do not see how it can be avoided. When we are able to say that we have secured the men who can do the work, and do it well, I think we are fairly entitled to ask parliament to pay those men according to the work they do and the responsibility they have assumed. As to the other men who may have equal qualifications, it is to be hoped that in due time their turn will come.
That is small consolation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It may be; but we think that the recognition of merit by rapid promotion does not tend to inefficiency in the service. I would think quite the contrary, and it is efficiency in the service which the country is particularly desirous of securing.

I think it tends to great inefficiency. Within the past few years we have had in this House frequent inquiries, in passing the estimates, why certain appointees have had their salaries increased in abnormal proportions and have been promoted over the heads of those much older in the service, and we have never had any other reason given than that advanced to-night, namely, that the men are efficient and that the object is to secure the services of efficient men by promotions of that kind. And we will never have any other reason until our civil service is reorganized on a proper basis, and the public are awaiting with much interest the Bill which is to provide for a reform. They are waiting to find out whether that Bill will incorporate the valuable suggestions and proposals of reform contained in the report of the Civil Service Commissioners, which has been so universally condemned by the friends of the government and the Liberal press. In the city of Montreal there are efficient civil servants, but examples are



frequent beyond number of appointees of the present government being promoted over old employees, not appointed by the preceding government particularly, but whose nominations frequently date back to the; time of the Mackenzie administration. As a consequence our postal service in Montreal, which gives the second largest revenue of any city in the Dominion, is very largely disorganized. It is not because the men are not as a rule good men. They are of course very insufficiently paid, but the disorganization is due to the system of promotions, for which no satisfactory reasons can be given. Within the past few months a system has been inaugurated of putting comparatively recent postal employees- friends no doubt of the Postmaster General -thtrough a sham examination, and then promoting them over men who have given faithful service during a much greater number of years. That is one of the reasons why the postal service in Montreal is not at all satisfactory, and it never will be until we have the system established which 1ms been in force in England since 1857 and is also in force in the Post Office Department in the United States. Appointments are there only made by a commission after an examination, and the question of patronage is eliminated altogether, and promotions are only made .after examination and under certain conditions. I do not mean to say that the two men, to whom reference has been made, are not efficient, but they have been promoted over the heads of men who have been far longer in the service, whose salaries remain comparatively stationary and who get no chance to compete for the higher grades. The Minister of the Interior thinks that that system promotes efficiency, but the experience of the. civil servants themselves and the public is absolutely in the contrary direction.
What are the duties of Mr. E. H. Wright and what is his salary?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Wright is the chief assistant commissioner of Dominion lands and his salary is $1,550.
Mr. FOSTER, When did he get that? $1,250 is what is down here for the last year and that with the annual increase would mean $1,300 now.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that he was made a first-class clerk in 1906.
What was his salary in 1901?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say. He entered the service in June, 1893, and was made permanent in 1894.
He advanced very rapidly. I think his salary was $600 in 1901. Has he special aptitude for the work?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Commissioner of Dominion Lands is of course the most respou-Mr. MONK.
sible official in the department and Mr. Wright is his chief assistant. Mr. Green-wray, the commissioner, handles a large number of land matters and requires some four or five men to assist n!m. Mr. Wright is the chief of those assistants.
He went ahead very rapidly.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I need not say to the House how very important is the work he does. It is not routine w ork in any sense, but work that requires the exercise of the very best judgment and decision, as well as thorough familiarity not only with the Land Act, but also with the actual operation of homesteading upon the land. It seem that in the stress of work Mr. Wright has been able to show that of Mr. Green-way's assistants he was the better man.
How does he show it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: By reason of his ability in arriving at correct decisions promptly, I presume.
You presume?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I say by reason of his arriving promptly at correct decisions to the satisfaction of the commissioner and the minister. I understood the hon. gentleman to say that Mr. Wright had been appointed in 1903.

As a member who perhaps has as much to do with that branch as any other member, if not more, I wish to take exception to what the member for Toronto (Mr. Kemp) says. I think that the salary should be more. In the first place after fifteen years' service $1,500 is not out of the way when expenses have increased so.
I was not taking exception to the amount of the salary, I was inquiring to the reason for the rapid advance.

I have a great deal of correspondence with that department as well as personal intercourse, and I find that Mr. Wright has a wonderful grasp of its affairs, he has an ability for doing his work with great accuracy and I would consider that the government secured his services very cheaply at $1,550.

The difficulty is that there appears to be no principle upon which these rapid advances are made, which does not tend to the efficiency of the service. It is absurd to suppose that men who have been long in the service are inefficient, as they must have been efficient when they entered, for they passed the examinations, and they have since added experience. The explanation is that those who have recently entered the service through political influence have their friends still alive and influential and able to secure their advancement.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend's suggestion is absolutely gratuitous. The explanations that have been given are absolutely correct. These men were promoted because of their efficiency in the service and that was the only reason, not because they had any political pull. Length of service in a department does not necessarily tend to efficiency any more than in a private business. It must be apparent to any one that the man who has had to fight the battle of life in the world at large, has to take his chance with competitors in all lines on entering the department, other things being equal, is more likely to be efficient than the man who knows nothing except what he has learned within the four walls of a department. The suggestion that a commission should regulate the advancement of these men is another means of arriving at the same result. Working in the interests of the public and for the efficiency of the service they would take the responsibility of picking out the efficient men and passing them to the head of the list. The only difference is that now the minister takes that responsibility and so far as these men are concerned I accept the fullest responsibility.
That is a very pretty theory of the minister, but it does not hold in this case. I watched the whole process, how it resolved itself

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman say that what I said is not true?

I am going to say what I think is true and we can compare the two. He says take a man in the vortex of life, thrown hither and thither, his muscles toughened mentally and otherwise and when you get such a man you must promote him quickly. Let us take these two paragons.	Here is Mr. Wright. Howmuch of a vortex had he been in before he entered the department and became old and moss-covered? He entered the department as messenger in 1893, he was a third-class clerk in 1901, a second class clerk in 1905, a first-class clerk in 1907 and is still going upward. The fine theory does not fit in with this particular case. Mr. Wright was the nominee and favourite of a minister, the late Hon. Mr. Sutherland had him made a messenger and during his life carefully shoved him upwards.
In the case of Mr. Roberts, Mr. Calvert carefully shoves him upwards. Who is the good genius behind Mr. Marchand?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I wish to have this question settled first. I did not suggest that there was no way of getting good service except by taking men from the outside. I said that, other things being equal, you were more likely to get capable and efficient men from the outside. I did not suggest that you could not get good men with-308J
in the service. Mr. Wright is one who has acquired his experience within the department but yet has proven himself efficient.
I do not understand the suggestion that Mr. Wright entered the service as a protege of Mr. Sutherland, the minister. Mr. Sutherland was not a minister in 1893.
But he became a minister afterwards, he was a member of parliament. He had a great deal of influence.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then he must have had a great deal of judgment in the selection of a messenger in this case at any rate. I think the argument of my hon. friend falls to the ground in the case of Mr. Wright.
And is entitled to promotion ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That may be. The House has the evidence that the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Knowles) that in the position which he occupies to-day-and I wish to say the same emphatically and from my own knowledge of the case-he is a thoroughly efficient employee.
I am not saying he is not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The proposal placed before the House is thoroughly warranted in liis case. Mr. Marchand is assistant accountant of the department. The accountancy is held by Mr. Beddoe. The branch, of course, is a large one. I need not say to the House that the question of accounting is a very important question. There are nineteen officials in the accounting branch. The Department of the Interior has business scattered all the way from Ottawa to Dawson city, and, in the proper conduct of that business, it has been found necessary, ever since I have been minister, to employ the services of the chief accountant, Mr. Beddoe, at distant points on several occasions. At the present time he is in Winnipeg, attending to the accounting in connection with the seed grain. It seems to me necessary to the service that there should be not only a chief accountant, but, when that chief accountant is necessarily absent, there should be some one to take his place-there should be an assistant or deputy
And he should be a chief clerk ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
-and he should have rank and pay according to his abilities and responsibilities. I have stated that point before; it does no harm to emphasize it; if we are to have efficient service aud to retain men who have proven themselves efficient, we must pay those men fair and reasonable salaries. It is on that principle that I ask for the promotion of Mr. Mar-

chand to the rank and position and salary which I have asked.

For my part, I think that the observations of the minister about the ' vortex ' and about the results of this ' vortex ' and its qualifying effects upon the new appointees, is not taken seriously by anybody. For, the presumption is that those who have served faithfully for many years, are entitled to promotion and advancement rather than to have men taken out of the ' vortex ' who have not had equal experience. Until we get a reform of the civil service, such as many people of this country have been looking for for many years-and we seem to be on the eve of it, if the government

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How long have the people been looking for that reform ?
For my part, I have combatted in favour of that reform since I have been a member of this House, and I have been a member as long as the Minister of Finance has.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I have not heard my hon. friend (Mr. Monk).

-ot a single session has passed in which I have not pointed out the enormous difference between what is going on in this country and what goes on in every other civilized country of the world. As far back as ten years ago, I pointed out the improvements wrought in England and have named the books in which these improvements are clearly shown. I have shown the immense work, which, since 1882, has been going on in the same direction in the United States, while we have been steadily retrograding since twelve 1 ears. And a few days before the report of the commission was brought in, I used strong expressions in this House. I stated that our civil service at the present moment was rotten, worthless, and I hoped that the report which was then being worked out-and which, I fancy, was then a subject of some anxiety to the Minister of Finance-would give us relief. But this government, and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, resemble the Pharaohs of Ancient Egypt. Under those kings, messengers who brought bad news were condemned to death, while those who brought good news were covered with flowers. Take this very instance; when cases of this kind come up the minister blames those who criticise the estimates as though they were trying to prevent the promotion and advancement of the particular civil servant whose case was being considered. Nothing has been said by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) that would imply that. I do not know that these parti-Mr. OLIVER.	I; . J *
cular men whose salaries are up for consideration are unfitted for promotion. But I say it is strange that, in every case, in the last twelve years, where anomalies of this kind have been pointed out, the answer of the minister has always been that the officer was promoted for efficiency- ' How is that efficiency as compared with that of other men in the service -' I am the judge of it ; I take the fullest responsibility for what it is proposed to do.' And that is all the satisfaction we get. I think that the only way to bring about this urgent and absolutely essential reform is to point out the conditions in every case until the government finds itself obliged to promote instead of retarding that very essential reform. This Mr. Pierre Marchand was appointed on 12th of December, 1899. He came in at $1,100. At the present moment, he is first-class clerk and assistant accountant at $1,000. I find in the civil service list two other first-class clerks appointed before Mr. Marchand. There are Mr. Peter Robertson, appointed on February 27, 1877; and Mr. Geo. Dalrymple Pope, appointed March 31, 1884. There are also second-class clerks: Mr. James Dunnet, appointed April 1, 1878 ; Mr. Samuel J. Willoughby, appointed January 12, 1886 ; and Mr. Henry Hamish Turner, appointed June 20, 1883. These are old civil servants. Are they inefficient as compared with the more recent appointees ? Does it not seem to the members of this committee that these men, if equally efficient, on account of priority of appointment ought to receive promotion, or ought to be given the chance which any properly organized civil service should give of obtaining promotion, rather than promote more recent appointees ? My hon. friend would lead the committee to believe that, taking a new man and advancing him rapidly over the heads of old employees-whom we. must presume to be efficient and capable men-is a valuable method of insuring the efficiency of the service. I think we are approaching a period of reform. I regret very much to see the spirit in which the government has received .the most valuable suggestions made under the most favourable circumstances for the government by the commissioners. I await with anxiety the measure which has been proposed and in which I hope to find the valuable suggestions referred to carried out. But, until that point is reached I will take every opportunity of pointing out to the committee and of making known to the public what I consider to be the cause of the insufficiency, as I find it, in the civil service in the province of Quebec in order to hurrv up that reform.

The minister is not altogether consistent in this matter for at one

moment lie pleads that the large number of employees in his department is some excuse why justice should not be done in all matters appertaining to these promotions. The next moment he pleads that it is owing to the efficiency of these particular clerks that they are promoted. I do not see what the enormous number of employees has to do with this question at all because the minister only has to consider seventeen men in attending to the promotion of these two clerks. You will find there are two of these first-class clerks who are already in receipt of a salary of $1,900, and there are two already in receipt of a salary of $1,850. It does seem rather hard that gentlemen receiving the lowest salary of first-class clerks should be promoted over those who have been so much longer in the service as to be entitled to larger salaries. Mr. Marchand is receiving $1,600 and Mr. Roberts is receiving $1,500. They are selected and placed above other clerks who are in receipt of larger salaries. These men of large experience are at the top of the tree, in so far as first-class clerks are concerned and can receive no more salary, while Mr. Roberts is given an immediate advance of $-100 with the probability of next year receiving $2,300. It does seem to me that there is ground for the remarks of the hon. member for North Toronto, and there must be some reason why this rapid advancement is taking place in the matter of these two promotions.
Are there any other promotions ? I see there are 26 second-class clerks, while last year there were 25. Who is the 26th?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is to give promotion to the second class of Mr. A. R. Mor-risset of the accountant's branch.
Where is he now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is a junior second-class clerk at $1,050.
When was he appointed, and at what salary?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He was appointed a tern porary clerk in 1898 at $400.
Has he undergone the civil service examination?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
When was his first promotion?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He was appointed on the 1st of July, 1898, and he was appointed to the permanent staff on the 1st July, 1901. He is attached to the accountant's branch as a junior second-class clerk.
What was his salary in 1901?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: What salary will he get as a second-class clerk?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: $1,200. He was appointed on the 1st July, 1901, at $600 as a junior second-class clerk and in 1903 the salary of iuniors was raised from $600 to $800.

We find in this case an exact parallel if not a little more than a parallel. In 1898 Mr. Morrisett was appointed a temporary clerk at $400; in 1901 he was appointed a permanent clerk at $600, and in 1903 there was an increase in his salary. He then got $1,050 and under this vote he will get $1,200. In less than ten years he has gone from $400 to $1,200. Here are four samples that we have unearthed by a little process of questioning, every one of these have been placed in office by the government at low salaries and have been rushed forward, two of them to be chief clerks and one to be a second-class clerk. The remarks made by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) are altogether to the point in this respect.

I would like to ask the minister if Peter Robertson, George Dalry-mple Pope, James Dunnet, Samuel J. Willoughby, Henry Hamish Turner, who are older employees than Mr. Marchand or Mr. Roberts are good and efficient employees ?
I do not know these men, but I would like to get that information from the minister. They have quite considerable salaries ranging from $1,300 to $1,600, and they occupy positions in the service as first and second-class clerks. Are they good and efficient men?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will have to ask the deputy in regard to the qualifications of these men. It is impossible for me to have knowledge of the qualifications of all the members of the service. But while these men may be perfectly competent, trustworthy and reliable in every way in the positions which they occupy they still may not be competent to take part of the supervision of the transactions of the accountant's branch as we expect the assistant accountant to do. These gentlemen are being paid for work which they are able to do aud do well, but that is no evidence that they are fit for a position of supervision.
It all goes to show that these promotions ought not to be in the hands of the minister but in the hands of a commission who would make promotions under certain changeable rules.
As it was before 1896.

That is a very small idea. There is no doubt this system has existed since confederation and like all rotten

systems it has become aggravated year after year. X do not care what was done previously, this is a question of essential reform that ought to be carried out. The Minister of the Interior is not able to tell us whether older and efficient employees are fit for the position, and yet he says this is an excellent mode of carrying on the civil service.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I said I thought this was an efficient way of getting an efficient service, but I did not say there could not be a better mode. Even if we had a most conscientious Civil Service Commission there would sometimes be occasion for such appointments where men would get rapid promotion because of special efficiency and there would be the same grievance on the part of men who were longer in the service, who were doing the work they were at efficiently, but who were not specially qualified for the more important duties. I am aware of the propriety of the appointments we are asking the House to sanction, I admit I am not aware of how good other appointments might be.

That is frank but it shows this is the worst possible system that could prevail. The effect of that system is to keep out of the public service good men and to chase out of it some of the very best men in the service.
Have the civil servants in the Interior Department been paid for the past month?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Sixty per cent of their salary was paid on the 10th.

What appears to be a little strange is that when the difficulty supervened which I regret had been caused by the government in regard to the voting of supplies, some method should not have been made to place in a distinct column separate from the rest of Supply, the necessary vote for the payment of civil servants. It is a great pity that is not done every year and it is a great pity it was not done this year when these grave difficulties at first appeared. For my part I think the civil servants should all be paid regularly and I would have raised no objection to that. The estimates have been made up in this form for years and I will admit for the benefit of my friend from Vercheres (Mr. Geoffrion) they were made up in that way before his party came to power, if he thinks that is any reason why we should check all progress. I regret very much that we are not in a position to vote the salaries of the civil servants as they should be voted, without difficulty, and I attribute that to the careless way in which the estimates are made up. When these difficulties first arose a division of the estimates should have been made so that the salaries of the civil servants would have been voted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is so zealous for these civil servants why has he been opposing this vote for the last half hour?
That remark is childish.
I am surprised at the Minister of Finance making such a statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from Montreal (Mr. Monk) professes zeal for the passage of the civil service estimates, but on the other hand he has been delaying them.
Does the Minister of Finance in this age think he can induce people to believe that we are to pass estimates without the fair and reasonable questioning on them that we have had to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The estimates have been held up all day.

Here is $190,000 being voted and we have spent 25 minutes asking proper questions, and the Minister of Finance rises in a temper to lecture us because we have dared in the face of his high mightiness to ask for information with reference to these inordinate galloping promotions. If the Minister of Finance takes that line he is most foolish.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am responsible for what I said and not for what the hon. gentleman attributes to me. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier was indulging in sympathy for the civil servants who did not get their money, and I pointed out that the reason for that was because hon. gentleman opposite had been delaying these estimates, not for to-night, but for weeks and months.

And I have to state to the Minister of Finance that I pleaded with him and with his chief to take up these civil government estimates three weeks ago but he stuck up the Minister of Public Works before the civil servants and the opposition and voted hundreds of thousands of dollars for public works which are not necessary at the present time. That is what was done and that is what is on record on ' Hansard.' The minister has been playing to the gallery long enough. He is played out, perfectly played out. Small boys in debating societies play that sort of game ; the Minister of Finance ought to have wisdom enough not to play it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall not undertake to speak of what took place between the leaders; I only speak of that which I know, and when the hon. gentleman says he offered to give the civil government estimates, I venture to say that the hon. gentleman is mistaken.
I venture to say that he is right, and * Hansard ' will prove it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: ' Hansard ' will prove nothing except constant obstruction. If the hon. gentleman wants to give the civil service estimates, why does he not give them, instead of spending all day on a matter that has no bearing on the business of the House ? The hon. gentleman must remember that the civil service is not confined to civil government at Ottawa but is scattered all over Canada.

And if the Prime Minister and his first lieutenant had shown ordinary political diligence, they would have had their large measures down before the sixth or seventh month of the session, and they would have had the estimates which they do not have now, from that very speeding of the business which they might well have done. The Minister of the Interior has all his civil government, now, including the Indian Department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What is the business for to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Supply, with the estimates of the Minister of the Interior.
When are we going to have the Civil Service Bill explained ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend any definite statement.
Is it on account of the necessary absence of the Minister of Agriculture ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The absence of the Minister of Agriculture is as necessary as that of many other hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House.
But he is a minister ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are all members here, and we speak as members more than as ministers, and the absence of one member is not to be censured more than the absence of another.

Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.05 a.m., Wednesday.
cancellation of the resolution adopted the 20th of May last, by which the House adopted the fourth report of the committee appointed to supervise the official debates of the House. I beg to move :
That the resolution adopted by this House on the 20th of May last adopting the fourth report of the committee appointed to supervise the official debates of the House, be reconsidered and rescinded; that the said fourth report of the said committee be referred back to said committee with instructions to inquire into the necessity of and demand for said additional translator and the qualifications of said E. Charlier to act as such translator and to be appointed to such new position and to inquire also as to such additional measures as may be necessary to ensure the prompt and efficient translation of the official documents of this House.
I would have given notice to my hon. friend, the member of St. James division (Mr. Gervais) who is chairman of that committee, but he has not been in the House lately. In fact, I do not think he has been here since the adoption of the fourth report in question. Nevertheless, with the unanimous consent of the House, the motion may be disposed of now. I do not think there is any doubt, from what has transpired since that fourth report was adopted, that the report must be reconsidered. It was adopted under the erroneous impression that it involved no additional expense. 1 shall present the motion, if my right hon. friend consents, or leave it as a notice of motion.
I would prefer that it should stand as a notice. I can talk with my hon. friend during the day and perhaps, fix a day for moving it.
As the matter has been some time in abeyance, it is urgent that the motion should be presented to-morrow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps. I shall see my hon. friend during the day.
